concepts.title: Data Types and Variables
concepts.description: JavaScript's values split into primitives (compared and copied by value) and reference types (compared and copied by reference), and understanding typeof, coercion, and truthy/falsy rules head off many common JS bugs.
learningObjectives: Distinguish primitive types from reference types and explain why that distinction determines how values are compared and copied.
Predict the result of typeof for any given value, including the typeof null quirk.
Explain why == performs coercion and === does not, and predict the result of common == comparisons.
List the six falsy values in JavaScript and correctly classify any given value as truthy or falsy.

sections.heading: Primitives vs Reference Types
sections.body:
JavaScript values fall into two categories, and most 'why did this variable change when I didn't touch it' bugs come from confusing the two. **Primitive types** (`string`, `number`, `boolean`, `null`, `undefined`, `symbol`, and `bigint`) are immutable and compared/copied **by value**. When you write `let b = a` for a primitive `a`, `b` gets its own independent copy of that value; changing `b` afterward never affects `a`.

**Reference types** (objects, arrays, and functions) are everything else. Arrays and functions are specialized objects, not separate kinds of thing (an array is an object whose keys happen to be numeric-like strings plus a special `length` property; a function is an object you can call). All reference types are compared and copied **by reference**: a variable holding an object doesn't hold the object itself, it holds a pointer to where that object lives in memory. `let b = a` for an object copies the *pointer*, not the object -- so `a` and `b` point at the same object, and mutating through one is visible through the other. The Arrays and Objects concepts cover this aliasing in depth; the root cause is this primitive-vs-reference split.

sections.heading: typeof and Its Quirks
sections.body:
The `typeof` operator returns a string naming a value's type, and it's mostly intuitive: `typeof "hi"` is `"string"`, `typeof 42` is `"number"`, `typeof true` is `"boolean"`, `typeof undefined` is `"undefined"`, `typeof Symbol()` is `"symbol"`, `typeof 10n` is `"bigint"`. Then there are the exceptions.

The most famous gotcha in the language: **`typeof null` returns `"object"`**, not `"null"`. This is a bug from JavaScript's first implementation in 1995 (values were tagged internally, and `null` was represented with the same tag as objects); it has never been fixed because fixing it would break an enormous amount of existing code across the web, so it's now permanent. In practice, never use `typeof x === "object"` alone to check for 'this is a real object': it also matches `null`, so add `x !== null`.

Two more quirks: `typeof` on a function returns `"function"`, even though a function is an object under the hood (functions get their own result because checking for callability is so common). And `typeof` on an array returns `"object"`, not `"array"`: there is no array result, which is why checking for arrays needs a different tool (covered in the Arrays concept).

sections.heading: Type Coercion: == vs ===
sections.body:
JavaScript has two equality operators that look almost identical but behave differently. `==` (loose equality) will **coerce** (convert) operands to a common type before comparing if they're different types -- `"5" == 5` is `true` because the string gets converted to a number first; `null == undefined` is `true` because the spec treats those two as loosely equal to each other (and to nothing else); `0 == false` is `true` because `false` coerces to `0`. These coercion rules are hard to memorize in full (the classic `[] == false` is also `true`, via a chain of conversions most people can't recite), and that is the problem.

`===` (strict equality) never coerces: it only returns `true` if both operands are already the same type **and** the same value. `"5" === 5` is `false`. `null === undefined` is `false`. This is why `===` is the default for nearly all comparisons in modern JavaScript: it does what it looks like it does, with no hidden conversion table, which avoids a whole category of 'why is this weirdly true/false' bugs. Reach for `==` only when you want `null` or `undefined` to match either value; `x == null` is the one common legitimate use of `==` in well-reviewed modern code.

sections.heading: Truthy and Falsy Values
sections.body: Any value can be used where a boolean is expected (an `if` condition, a `&&`/`||` expression, a ternary), and JavaScript converts it to `true` or `false` by fixed rules. Memorize the short list of **six** everyday falsy values: `false`, `0` (and `-0`), `""` (the empty string), `null`, `undefined`, and `NaN`. (Strictly there are two more: the BigInt zero `0n`, and the legacy `document.all` in browsers. You will rarely meet either.) Everything else is truthy, including values that feel like they 'should' be empty or false: the string `"0"` (non-empty, so truthy), the string `"false"` (same reason), and **every object and array, even an empty one**. `if ([])` and `if ({})` both run their body, because an empty array or object is still an object reference. This causes bugs when someone writes `if (myArray)` intending to check 'is this array non-empty': that check passes whenever `myArray` is an array at all. The correct check is `if (myArray.length > 0)`.

examples.title: typeof Across Every Type
examples.code:
console.log(typeof "hello");     // "string"
console.log(typeof 42);          // "number"
console.log(typeof true);        // "boolean"
console.log(typeof undefined);   // "undefined"
console.log(typeof null);        // "object", the famous bug
console.log(typeof Symbol());    // "symbol"
console.log(typeof 10n);         // "bigint"
console.log(typeof function(){}); // "function"
console.log(typeof []);          // "object"  -- not "array"
console.log(typeof {});          // "object"
examples.explanation: Every primitive gets an accurate typeof label except one: null reports "object" because of a decades-old implementation bug that's now permanent for backward compatibility. Functions get their own "function" result even though they're objects, because 'is this callable' is a common check. Arrays report plain "object"; typeof has no 'array' result, which is why Array.isArray exists as a separate check (covered in the Arrays concept).

examples.title: == Coercion Surprises vs === Predictability
examples.code:
console.log("5" == 5);         // true  -- string coerced to number
console.log("5" === 5);        // false -- different types, no coercion
console.log(null == undefined);  // true  -- special-cased pair
console.log(null === undefined); // false
console.log(0 == false);       // true  -- false coerces to 0
console.log(0 === false);      // false
console.log([] == false);      // true  -- coercion chain most people can't recite
console.log([] === false);     // false
examples.explanation: Every == line performs a hidden conversion before comparing, and the rules for what converts to what are obscure. [] == false is true because [] first converts to a primitive (via its default string conversion, becoming ""), then "" == false converts both sides to 0, and 0 == 0 is true. Nobody should need to trace that chain to read ordinary code. Every === line just asks 'same type, same value?' with no conversion, which is why it's the default choice.

misconceptions.description: typeof null returning "object" means null is actually a kind of object in JavaScript.
misconceptions.clarification: null is a primitive value, one of the seven primitive types, and it represents 'intentionally no value.' typeof null reporting "object" is a documented bug from JavaScript's original 1995 implementation, kept because fixing it would break existing code across the web that depends on it. A typeof x === "object" check is not enough for 'x is a real object'; also check x !== null.

misconceptions.description: Empty arrays and objects are falsy, since they're 'empty' and represent nothing.
misconceptions.clarification: The everyday falsy values are false, 0, "", null, undefined, and NaN (plus 0n and the legacy document.all). An array or object is a reference type, and every object reference, including [] and {}, is truthy, no matter what it contains or how 'empty' it looks. if (myArray) only tells you myArray exists and is not null/undefined; it says nothing about whether it has any elements. To check for emptiness, test myArray.length === 0 (or Object.keys(myObj).length === 0 for a plain object).

exercises.prompt: What does each line print?
hints: typeof null is one of the most famous exceptions in the language: it doesn't report what you'd expect.
null and undefined are special-cased against each other for ==, but === doesn't share that rule.
For "" == 0, think about what an empty string coerces to when compared against a number, and remember === never coerces.
exercises.expectedAnswer: "object" (the typeof null bug); true (null == undefined is specially allowed); false (=== never coerces, and they are different types/values); true ("" coerces to 0 for ==); false (different types, === never coerces).
exercises.solutionExplanation: typeof null is "object" due to a permanent legacy bug, not because null is an object. null == undefined is true because the spec treats those two values as loosely equal only to each other (and nothing else), but null === undefined is false because === requires identical types, and null and undefined are different types. "" == 0 is true because == coerces the empty string to the number 0 before comparing, and 0 == 0 is true; "" === 0 is false because === never coerces a string into a number, so a string can never strictly equal a number.

exercises.prompt: This function is supposed to skip processing when passed an empty array, but it processes empty arrays anyway and crashes on items[0].toUpperCase(). Find and fix the bug.
hints: !items only checks whether items itself is falsy (e.g. null, undefined). What truthiness does an array have, regardless of how many elements it contains?
An empty array [] is still an array reference, not a falsy value, so !items is false for it and the function keeps going.
What you want to check is whether the array has zero elements, which is a property of the array, not of its truthiness.
exercises.solutionExplanation: !items only guards against items being null, undefined, or another falsy value; it does nothing for an empty array, because [] is a truthy object reference no matter how many elements it holds. The !items check passes for [], so execution reaches items[0].toUpperCase(), and items[0] is undefined (reading an out-of-range index gives undefined, not an error). Calling .toUpperCase() on undefined then throws. Adding items.length === 0 checks the condition the function cares about, 'does this array have anything in it,' which truthiness can't answer for a reference type.

assessments.prompt: Which of these values is truthy (evaluates to true in a boolean context)?
options: NaN
[] (an empty array)
"" (an empty string)
assessments.explanation: The everyday falsy values are false, 0, "", null, undefined, and NaN, and the other three options are all on that list. [] is an array, which is a reference type, and every object/array reference is truthy regardless of its contents, so an empty array is truthy even though it 'contains nothing.' This is why if (arr) is not a valid way to check for an empty array; use arr.length > 0 instead.

assessments.prompt: A teammate writes `if (typeof value === "object")` intending to check that `value` is a real object before calling `Object.keys(value)` on it. Explain what's wrong with this check and how to fix it.
assessments.modelAnswer: The check is incomplete because typeof null also returns "object". This is a well-known, permanent bug from JavaScript's original implementation, not a sign that null is an object. So if value happens to be null, typeof value === "object" is true, the code proceeds to call Object.keys(null), and that throws a TypeError, because null isn't an object and has no keys. The fix is to exclude null alongside the typeof check: if (typeof value === "object" && value !== null). typeof also returns "object" for arrays (typeof [] is "object"), so if the intent is 'a plain object, not an array,' add !Array.isArray(value) as well; typeof can't distinguish objects from arrays.

concepts.title: Functions
concepts.description: Function declarations, function expressions, and arrow functions differ in hoisting behavior and, most importantly, in how they bind this, a distinction that shaped a decade of JavaScript UI code and still matters for reading it.
learningObjectives: Distinguish function declarations, function expressions, and arrow functions by syntax.
Predict which function forms can be called before their definition line runs, based on hoisting rules.
Explain how a regular function's this is determined by its call site, versus how an arrow function inherits this from its enclosing scope.
Predict when a callback will lose its intended this binding, and fix it with an arrow function or .bind().
Use default parameters correctly, including when they apply and when they don't.

sections.heading: Three Ways to Write a Function
sections.body: JavaScript gives you three syntaxes for creating a function, and although they are often interchangeable in simple cases, they are not equivalent. A **function declaration** starts with the `function` keyword as a statement and has its own name: `function add(a, b) { return a + b; }`. A **function expression** assigns an (often anonymous) function to a variable: `const add = function(a, b) { return a + b; };`. An **arrow function** uses a more compact `=>` syntax, also typically assigned to a variable: `const add = (a, b) => a + b;`. With a single expression body and no `{ }`, the value is returned implicitly; if you use `{ }` for the body, you need an explicit `return` again.

sections.heading: Hoisting Differences
this Binding: Regular Functions vs Arrow Functions
Default Parameters
sections.body:
Any parameter can have a default value, used whenever the corresponding argument is **`undefined`**. Falsy isn't enough:

```javascript
function greet(name = "Guest") {
  return "Hello, " + name;
}

greet();          // "Hello, Guest": no argument passed, so name is undefined and the default applies
greet(undefined); // "Hello, Guest": an explicit undefined still counts
greet(null);      // "Hello, null": null is not undefined, so the default does not apply
greet("");        // "Hello, ": an empty string is not undefined either
```

The `null` case is a common surprise: people expect default parameters to work like a 'fill in if falsy' fallback (as `??` does for `null` and `undefined`, covered later in this module), but they only trigger on `undefined`. Default expressions are evaluated on every call, at call time, and can reference earlier parameters in the same list: in `function makeRange(start, end = start + 10) { ... }`, calling `makeRange(5)` gives `end` the value `15`, computed from that call's `start`.

examples.title: Hoisting: Declaration vs Expression vs Arrow
examples.explanation: declared is a full function declaration, so its entire definition is hoisted to the top of the scope -- calling it before its written position in the file works as if it had been defined first. expressed is a const holding an arrow function; const declarations are hoisted into the temporal dead zone but not initialized, so calling expressed before its declaration line has run throws a ReferenceError, not a TypeError. The variable exists in a 'known about but off-limits' state and never becomes callable early the way a declaration does.

examples.title: this Lost in a Callback, Fixed with an Arrow Function
examples.explanation: Inside start, the callback passed to setInterval is an ordinary function, and setInterval invokes it as a plain callback, so its this is not timer (it is the global object in a browser, or a Timeout object in Node). this.seconds++ therefore produces NaN on that other object instead of incrementing timer.seconds. Inside startFixed, the callback is an arrow function, which has no this of its own -- it looks outward to its enclosing scope, which is the startFixed function body, whose this is timer (because startFixed itself was called as timer.startFixed()). The arrow function's this is fixed at definition time and doesn't change with how setInterval invokes it, which makes it reliable here.

misconceptions.description: Arrow functions are just shorter syntax for regular functions -- they behave identically, just with less typing.
misconceptions.clarification: Arrow functions differ in ways beyond syntax: they don't have their own this (they inherit it lexically from the enclosing scope, and it never changes based on call site); they don't have their own arguments object; and they cannot be used as constructors -- new MyArrow() throws a TypeError, because arrow functions have no [[Construct]] behavior and no prototype property. The this difference is the main reason to choose one form over the other for a given callback.

misconceptions.description: Since functions are hoisted in JavaScript, you can call any function, including one assigned to a const or let, before its definition line in the file.
misconceptions.clarification: Only function declarations (function foo() {...}) are hoisted with their full body, making them callable from above their own definition. A function expression or arrow function assigned to a variable is hoisted only according to that variable's own rule: var gives you undefined until the assignment line runs (calling it early throws TypeError: not a function), while let/const sit in the temporal dead zone and throw ReferenceError if accessed before their line executes. 'Functions are hoisted' is true only for the declaration form; as a shorthand it overstates what happens for the other two.

exercises.prompt: What happens when this code runs?
hints: The two function forms here differ: one is a declaration, the other is an expression assigned to a variable.
Only one of the two gets its whole body hoisted to the top of the scope; the other gets only its variable's hoisting.
const variables that haven't reached their declaration line yet are in the temporal dead zone -- what happens if you try to call one from there?
exercises.expectedAnswer: "Hello!" prints first (greet is a hoisted declaration, callable early), then a ReferenceError is thrown when calling farewell() -- 'Cannot access farewell before initialization' -- because farewell is a const still in the temporal dead zone at that point, so "Bye!" never prints.
exercises.solutionExplanation: greet is a function declaration, so its whole definition (name and body) is hoisted to the top of the module/script scope, and the call succeeds even though it appears above the function's written position. farewell is a const holding a function expression; const declarations are hoisted but not initialized, so the name farewell exists in the temporal dead zone from the top of the scope until its own declaration line executes. Calling farewell() before that line runs throws ReferenceError: Cannot access 'farewell' before initialization, and execution stops there, so the program never reaches the const farewell = ... line or logs "Bye!".

exercises.prompt: This click handler is supposed to log the button's own label each time it's clicked, but it always logs undefined. Find and fix the bug.
hints: addEventListener calls the handler itself, not as button.onClick(). What determines this in that kind of call?
A regular function's this depends on how it's called, not on where it was written or which object it was assigned onto.
Which of the two function forms doesn't have its own this at all, and keeps whatever this was where it was defined?
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original handler is a regular function, and addEventListener invokes it with this set to the element the listener is attached to (el), not button, so this.label is undefined. Rewriting the handler as an arrow function fixes it because an arrow function has no this of its own: it inherits this from attachHandler's body, and attachHandler was called as button.attachHandler(el), so this there is button. That captured this stays button however addEventListener later invokes the callback, which a regular function can't guarantee.

options: undefined, with no error
NaN or a TypeError
assessments.explanation: increment is a regular function, and this is determined by the call site, not by where the function was defined or assigned. extracted() is a bare function call (there's no object before the dot), so this inside it is undefined (in strict mode/modules, which is the default for most modern code) rather than counter. this.count then throws a TypeError (reading .count off undefined) or, in non-strict sloppy-mode code where this falls back to the global object, produces NaN (globalThis.count is undefined, and undefined + 1 is NaN). Either way, it is not 11: the object counter was never carried along with the extracted function reference.

assessments.prompt: Explain, to someone who has only ever used regular functions, what changes about this when a method is rewritten as an arrow function class property, and why that matters for passing it around as a callback.
assessments.modelAnswer: A regular function has its own this, and that this is decided at every call by the call site: called as obj.method(), this is obj; called through a bare reference, such as the same function stored in a variable and invoked directly, this is not obj anymore, even though it's the same function. This makes regular-function methods fragile the moment they're extracted and passed elsewhere as a callback (to setTimeout, to addEventListener, to .then()), because the new call site strips away the object context that this depended on. An arrow function has no this of its own. It looks outward to whatever this was in the scope where the arrow function was written, once, at definition time. So an arrow-function method (or a regular method whose body wraps its logic in an arrow-function callback) keeps referring to the same this however many times it's handed off and re-invoked by other code, because no call-site lookup happens on each call; it's fixed at creation like any other variable an arrow function closes over. This is why arrow functions became the standard way to write callbacks and event handlers that need to keep referring back to an enclosing object or component instance.

concepts.title: Arrays
concepts.description: Arrays are objects with numeric keys and a self-maintaining length property, not a distinct primitive type, and knowing which methods mutate in place versus which return a new array prevents many common array bugs.
learningObjectives: Explain that arrays are objects with numeric keys and a length property, not a separate primitive type.
Classify common array methods as mutating or non-mutating, and predict the state of the original array after each.
Predict the surprising result of sorting an array of numbers with the default sort() and explain why it happens.
Identify and fix the aliasing bug where two variables reference the same array.
Use Array.isArray() correctly to check whether a value is an array.

sections.heading: Arrays Are Objects
sections.body: An array is not a separate primitive type in JavaScript. It's a specialized object whose keys are non-negative integers written as strings under the hood (`arr[0]` is shorthand for the property named `"0"`), plus one automatically maintained property, `length`. `length` isn't computed by counting elements each time you read it. It's updated internally whenever you add or remove elements, and it normally equals one more than the highest numeric index present. This is why `typeof []` reports `"object"` (covered in the Data Types concept) rather than something array-specific, and why `arr.length = 0` works as an idiom for emptying an array in place: you're changing the property that defines how many elements the array has.

sections.heading: Mutating vs Non-Mutating Methods
sections.body:
Array methods fall into two camps, and mixing up which camp a method is in is a common source of bugs. **Mutating methods** change the original array in place and often return something other than a full new array: `push`/`pop` (add/remove from the end, return the new length / the removed item), `shift`/`unshift` (same but from the start), `splice` (remove/insert at an arbitrary position, returns the removed elements), `sort`, and `reverse`. **Non-mutating methods** leave the original array untouched and return a new array: `slice` (extract a range), `concat` (combine arrays), `map`, `filter` (covered in depth in a later concept), and the spread operator `[...arr]`.

The common surprise is `sort`. It looks like it gives you back a new ordered array, but it **mutates the array it's called on and also returns that same (now reordered) array**, so `const sorted = original.sort()` doesn't create a new array; `sorted` and `original` point at the same, mutated array. On top of that, `sort()` with no comparator sorts **as strings**, comparing each element's string form character by character, so `[10, 1, 2].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 2]`, not `[1, 2, 10]`: as strings, `"10"` sorts before `"2"` because `"1"` comes before `"2"`. Sorting numbers correctly requires an explicit comparator: `arr.sort((a, b) => a - b)`. Modern engines also have `arr.toSorted(...)`, which takes the same comparator but returns a sorted copy and leaves `arr` alone, so it avoids the mutation trap entirely (`toReversed()` and `toSpliced()` are the non-mutating counterparts of `reverse` and `splice`).

sections.heading: The Aliasing Bug
Checking For Arrays
sections.body: Because `typeof` reports `"object"` for arrays just as it does for plain objects, it can't distinguish the two, so you need a dedicated check. This matters in practice when an API sometimes returns a single object and sometimes a list. `Array.isArray(value)` returns `true` only for arrays, and it handles a case where `value instanceof Array` fails: an array created in a different browsing context, such as an iframe, has a different `Array` constructor, so `instanceof Array` can say `false` for a real array. `Array.isArray` doesn't depend on the constructor chain, so it isn't fooled. Use it whenever you need to branch on 'is this an array'.

examples.title: sort() Mutates and Sorts as Strings by Default
examples.explanation: sort() with no comparator converts each element to a string and compares lexicographically, so "10" sorts before "2" because "1" < "2" character by character. The result looks almost right, which makes this bug easy to miss. result === scores is true because sort() mutates the array in place and returns that same array reference, not a copy; there were never two arrays. Passing an explicit comparator, (a, b) => a - b, tells sort to compare numerically instead: it returns a negative number when a should come first, positive when b should, and 0 for a tie.

examples.title: Aliasing vs a Real Copy
examples.explanation: alias = cart copies the reference, not the array, so cart and alias are two names for one array. Pushing onto alias is the same as pushing onto cart, which is why cart shows the new "milk" entry. cart.slice() with no arguments returns a new array containing the same elements, so realCopy is separate from cart, and mutating it has no effect on cart. The fix for accidental aliasing is to create a new array explicitly (slice(), spread, or Array.from) instead of assigning the existing array to another name.

misconceptions.description: Array.prototype.sort() returns a new sorted array and leaves the original array untouched, the same way map or filter would.
misconceptions.clarification: sort() mutates the array it's called on in place and returns that same array reference; it does not create a new array. If you need the original array left untouched, copy it first: [...original].sort() or original.slice().sort(). Also remember sort()'s default comparison is string-based, not numeric, so sorting numbers correctly requires an explicit comparator function: arr.sort((a, b) => a - b).
misconceptions.fact: sort() mutates the array it's called on in place and returns that same array reference; it does not create a new array.

misconceptions.description: Writing const copy = originalArray creates an independent copy of the array.
misconceptions.clarification: Arrays are reference types, so const copy = originalArray only copies the reference: copy and originalArray point at the same array in memory. Mutating copy (via push, splice, sort, direct index assignment, or any other mutating operation) also changes what you see through originalArray, because there is only one array object involved, not two. An independent copy requires an explicit copying operation: originalArray.slice(), [...originalArray], or Array.from(originalArray).
misconceptions.fact: Arrays are reference types, so const copy = originalArray only copies the reference: copy and originalArray point at the same array in memory.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
hints: sort() with no arguments doesn't compare numbers the way you'd expect. What does it compare each element as?
Try comparing "100" and "25" character by character, the way string comparison works, rather than as the numbers 100 and 25.
Does sort() return a brand new array, or the same array it was called on?
exercises.expectedAnswer: [100, 25, 3, 9] -- sorted as strings, since "100" < "25" < "3" < "9" lexicographically. Then true, because sort() mutates and returns the same array object rather than creating a new one.
exercises.solutionExplanation: With no comparator, sort() converts every element to its string form and compares those strings character by character. "100" comes before "25" because '1' < '2'; "25" comes before "3" because '2' < '3'; "3" comes before "9" because '3' < '9' -- giving the final order [100, 25, 3, 9], not numeric order. ids === sorted is true because sort() mutates the array it's called on and returns that same reference, so there is one array in memory throughout this snippet, referenced by two variable names.

exercises.prompt: This function is supposed to return a shuffled copy of an array without changing the caller's original array, but it mutates the caller's array anyway. Find and fix the bug.
hints: const result = array -- does this line create a new array, or just a second name for the same one?
Since array and result refer to the same array object, swapping elements 'in result' is the same as swapping them in the caller's array.
You need a copying step before the swapping starts, something that produces a new array object.
exercises.solutionExplanation: const result = array is a plain aliasing assignment: it copies the reference, not the array, so result and array (and, in the caller, original) are three names for one array object. The swapping loop mutates that shared array, which is why the caller's original ends up shuffled even though the function only appears to touch result. Changing the first line to array.slice() creates a new array with the same elements, so result is independent of array/original and the loop only mutates the copy.

assessments.prompt: Which statement correctly describes how to check whether a value is an array?
options: Array.isArray(value)
typeof value === "array"
value.length !== undefined
value instanceof Object
assessments.explanation: Array.isArray() is the purpose-built check: it returns true only for arrays, including arrays created in a different iframe/context where instanceof Array can report false. typeof value === "array" never matches because typeof never returns "array"; arrays report "object". value instanceof Object is true for arrays but also for plain objects, dates, and most other reference types, so it doesn't isolate arrays. value.length !== undefined is unreliable because many non-arrays pass it (plain objects given a length property, or strings, which have a length).

assessments.prompt: Explain why `const b = a;` followed by `b.push(4)` changes what you see through `a`, when `a` and `b` look like two separate variables.
assessments.modelAnswer: Arrays are reference types in JavaScript, not primitives, so a variable holding an array doesn't hold the array's contents directly. It holds a reference (effectively a pointer) to where that array lives in memory. const b = a copies that reference, not the array, so a and b are two names for the same array object, and only one array was ever created in this snippet. Calling b.push(4) mutates that shared array in place; since a points at the same array, reading a afterward shows the mutation. Primitives behave differently: const y = x for a number or string produces two independent values. That's why an independent copy of an array needs an explicit copying operation like a.slice() or [...a], not a plain assignment.

concepts.title: Objects
concepts.description: Objects are reference types accessed by dot or bracket notation, assigning one to another aliases rather than copies it, and even a spread-based shallow copy still shares any nested objects with the original, a common source of bugs.
learningObjectives: Access object properties correctly with dot notation and bracket notation, and know when bracket notation is required.
Explain why assigning one object variable to another aliases the object rather than copying it.
Predict that a shallow copy (spread or Object.assign) still shares nested objects with the original, and identify the resulting bug.
Use computed property names to build object keys dynamically.

sections.heading: Object Literals and Property Access
sections.body: An object literal groups related data under named keys: `const user = { name: "Amara", age: 29 };`. You can read or write a property with **dot notation** (`user.name`) whenever the key is a fixed, valid identifier known at the time you write the code. **Bracket notation** (`user["name"]`) does the same thing but takes any expression, which makes it required where dot notation can't work: when the key is stored in a variable (`user[someVariable]`), when the key contains characters that aren't valid in an identifier (spaces, hyphens, or a key that starts with a digit, as in `user["first-name"]` and `user["2024-total"]`), or when the key is computed by an expression (`user["na" + "me"]`). Dot notation is a convenience for the common static-key case; bracket notation is the general form.

sections.heading: Objects Are References
Shallow Copy vs Deep Copy
sections.body:
To avoid the aliasing problem, you copy an object explicitly, most commonly with the spread operator: `const copy = { ...original };` (spread syntax is covered in a later concept, but this use is common enough to introduce here). This creates a new object, and reassigning a top-level property on `copy` does not affect `original`. The trap is that spread (and `Object.assign({}, original)`, which does the same thing) only copies **one level deep**. Any property whose value is itself an object or array is copied *by reference*, like the aliasing bug above, one level in:

```javascript
const original = { name: "Amara", address: { city: "Lagos" } };
const copy = { ...original };

copy.name = "Ben";              // fine, a top-level string is independent
console.log(original.name);     // still "Amara"

copy.address.city = "Nairobi";  // mutates the SHARED nested object
console.log(original.address.city);   // "Nairobi", changed too!
```

`copy.address` and `original.address` are still the same nested object, because the spread copied the *pointer* stored in `address`, not what it points to. This is a common bug: code that looks like it makes a safe copy before mutating, but still mutates shared nested state. A deep copy needs the built-in `structuredClone(original)` (modern JavaScript; it handles nested objects, arrays, Maps, and Sets), the older and lossier `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(original))` trick (it drops functions and `undefined` values, converts `Date` objects to strings, and throws on circular references), or a deep-clone utility.

sections.heading: Computed Property Names

examples.title: Dot vs Bracket Notation
examples.explanation: product.name works because name is a valid JavaScript identifier. product["unit-price"] is required for the second key because unit-price contains a hyphen, which dot notation would parse as subtraction rather than as part of a property name. product[key] is required whenever the key is stored in a variable rather than written literally: dot notation can't substitute a variable's value, since obj.something always means the property literally named something.

examples.title: Shallow Copy Still Shares Nested Objects
examples.explanation: { ...settings } creates a new outer object, so reassigning userSettings.theme only affects the copy -- theme is a primitive string, independent once copied. But userSettings.notifications was copied as a reference, so userSettings.notifications and settings.notifications are the same nested object; there is only one notifications object, so mutating it through either name shows up in both. safeCopy spreads the nested object too, giving notifications its own copy. Spreading every level you intend to mutate is the manual way to avoid shallow-copy bugs without a deep-clone utility.

misconceptions.description: Spreading an object with {...obj} makes a completely independent, deep copy -- nothing about the copy can ever affect the original.
misconceptions.clarification: {...obj} (and Object.assign({}, obj)) only copies one level deep. Top-level primitive properties become independent, but any property whose value is an object or array is copied by reference, so the copy and the original still point at the same nested object, and mutating a nested property through the copy also changes what the original sees. A deep copy needs structuredClone(obj), a recursive/library-based deep clone, or (with caveats around functions, undefined, and Dates) JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)).
misconceptions.fact: {...obj} (and Object.assign({}, obj)) only copies one level deep.

misconceptions.description: b = a; b.x = 5; doesn't affect a, because b is declared as its own separate variable.
misconceptions.clarification: Declaring b as a separate variable doesn't make it hold a separate object: for reference types, b = a copies the reference (a pointer to the object), not the object's data. a and b are two names for one object, so b.x = 5 mutates that object, and reading a.x afterward shows the change. Mutations through one are independent of the other only if a and b hold different objects, for example if b had been created with { ...a } instead of = a (and even then only one level deep, per the shallow-copy caveat).

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
hints: {...original} does copy something new, but think about how deep that copy goes.
profile's value is itself an object. Is that inner object copied, or just a reference to it?
If copy.profile and original.profile are still the same object underneath, what happens when you mutate a property on it through either name?
exercises.expectedAnswer: "Accra": the spread only shallow-copies, so copy.profile and original.profile are still the same nested object, and mutating it through copy also changes what original sees.
exercises.solutionExplanation: { ...original } creates a new outer object, but profile's value, itself an object, is copied by reference, not recreated. So copy.profile and original.profile point at the same nested object in memory. copy.profile.city = "Accra" mutates that one shared object's city property, and since original.profile is the same object, original.profile.city reflects the change too, even though original itself was never touched directly.

exercises.prompt: This function is supposed to return an updated copy of a user's preferences without ever mutating the caller's original object, but callers report their original preferences object keeps changing. Find and fix the bug.
hints: const updated = preferences -- does this create a new object, or just a second name for the same one?
Even if you fix that line with a spread, remember spread only copies one level deep. What about the nested display object?
You need to copy both the outer object and the specific nested object you're about to mutate.
exercises.solutionExplanation: const updated = preferences is a plain aliasing assignment, so updated.display.theme = newTheme mutates the object the caller passed in; there was never a copy at any level. Spreading only the outer object ({ ...preferences }) would not be enough, because display's value is itself an object and a shallow spread copies that nested reference, so updated.display.theme would still mutate preferences.display.theme. The fix spreads at both levels: the outer object gets its own copy, and display gets its own copy (via { ...preferences.display, theme: newTheme }) with theme overwritten on the new nested object, so the original's display object is never touched.

assessments.explanation: { ...a } creates a new outer object, so b.x = 100 only changes the copy's own top-level x -- a.x stays 1. But nested is copied by reference (spread is shallow), so b.nested and a.nested are the same object; b.nested.y = 200 mutates that shared object, so a.nested.y also reads as 200. The result is 1 200, the mixed outcome that makes shallow-copy bugs easy to miss: part of the object behaves as if fully copied, and part doesn't.

assessments.prompt: Explain why { ...obj } is called a 'shallow' copy, and describe a situation where that distinction causes a bug.
assessments.modelAnswer: { ...obj } creates a new object and copies obj's own top-level properties into it one by one. For a property whose value is a primitive (a string, number, boolean), that's a complete, independent copy: the new object gets its own value, unconnected to the original. But for a property whose value is itself an object or array, spread copies the reference to that value, not a new version of it, so the new outer object and the original still point at the same nested object. That's what 'shallow' means: only the first level of properties is duplicated, and anything nested deeper is still shared. A bug this causes: imagine a settings object like { theme: 'dark', notifications: { email: true } }, and code that does const draft = { ...settings } intending to let a user edit draft without affecting the saved settings until they explicitly save. If the user toggles draft.notifications.email, that mutates the one shared notifications object, so settings.notifications.email changes too, even though the user never 'saved' anything and the code never touched settings directly. The fix is either to spread every nested level you intend to mutate (draft.notifications would also need its own { ...settings.notifications } copy) or to use a deep-copy tool like structuredClone.

concepts.title: Destructuring, Spread, and Rest
concepts.description: Destructuring pulls values out of arrays and objects into named variables, spread expands an iterable or object into individual elements, and rest collects remaining arguments into a real array. You will see this syntax throughout React code.
learningObjectives: Destructure values out of arrays and objects, including with default values and renaming.
Use the spread operator to expand an array or object into a new array/object literal or into function call arguments.
Use rest parameters to collect a variable number of trailing function arguments into a real array.
Explain the difference between the spread operator and rest parameters despite their identical ... syntax.

sections.heading: Array and Object Destructuring
sections.body: **Destructuring** lets you pull values out of an array or object directly into named variables in a single statement, instead of accessing each one individually. Array destructuring matches by **position**: `const [first, second] = ["a", "b", "c"]` gives `first = "a"`, `second = "b"` (the third element is left unmatched). You can skip elements with a blank comma slot: `const [, second] = ["a", "b"]` gets just `"b"`. Object destructuring matches by **key name**, not position: `const { name, age } = { age: 29, name: "Amara" }` gets `name = "Amara"` and `age = 29` regardless of the order the properties appear in the source object. Both forms nest: `const { address: { city } } = user` reaches into a nested object directly, and `const [[a, b], [c, d]] = pairs` destructures a nested array.

sections.heading: Default Values and Renaming
sections.body:
Destructuring can supply a fallback for when the matched value is `undefined` (the same 'only undefined triggers it' rule as default parameters, covered in the Functions concept): `const [a = 1] = []` gives `a = 1`, since there's nothing at index 0; `const { timeout = 5000 } = options` gives `timeout` a default when `options` doesn't specify one.

Object destructuring can also **rename** a property into a different local variable name using a colon: `const { name: userName } = user` reads the `name` property but binds it to a local variable called `userName`, not `name`. Renaming and defaults combine: `const { name: userName = "Guest" } = user`. This is useful when destructuring two objects that happen to share a property name (`const { id: userId } = user; const { id: postId } = post;`), or when a property name would collide with a keyword or an already-used variable.

sections.heading: The Spread Operator
sections.body: The spread operator, `...`, expands an iterable or object into individual elements, in three common contexts. Inside an **array literal**: `[...arr1, ...arr2]` concatenates two arrays into a new one; `[...arr, newItem]` appends without mutating the original (contrast with `push`, which mutates). Inside an **object literal**: `{ ...obj1, ...obj2 }` merges properties from both into a new object. If both have the same key, **the later spread wins**; `{ ...obj, updatedField: newValue }` is the standard idiom for producing an updated copy of an object without mutating the original (and remember, per the Objects concept, this merge is still only shallow). In a **function call**: `Math.max(...numbers)` unpacks an array into individual arguments, as if you'd written each one out by hand. That helps with any function that takes separate arguments rather than one array.

sections.heading: Rest Parameters
sections.body: **Rest parameters** use the same `...` syntax but in the opposite direction: in a function's parameter list, they *collect* any remaining arguments into a real array rather than expanding something. (The same `...` also works at the end of a destructuring pattern, as in `const [head, ...tail] = list`.) `function sum(first, ...rest) { ... }` called as `sum(1, 2, 3, 4)` gives `first = 1` and `rest = [2, 3, 4]`, a real `Array` with every array method available (`.map`, `.reduce`, `.length`, and so on). This improves on the pre-ES6 way of handling variable arguments, the built-in `arguments` object. `arguments` is only *array-like* (it has a `.length` and numeric indices, but no `.map`/`.filter`/`.reduce`, so you'd have to convert it first), it includes every argument rather than letting you separate out named ones the way `first, ...rest` does, and **arrow functions don't have their own `arguments` object** (like `this`, per the Functions concept). Rest parameters work in every function form.

sections.heading: Why This Matters for React
sections.body: Destructuring and spread show up constantly in React code, from the first component you write. Destructuring a component's `props` object in the signature, `function UserCard({ name, avatarUrl, isOnline })`, is the standard way to declare what data a component expects, instead of writing `props.name` throughout the body. Spreading props, `<Avatar {...userProps} />`, forwards a whole object of props to a child in one expression. And the 'copy with one field changed' idiom from the spread section, `{ ...state, count: state.count + 1 }`, is how state updates are written throughout React, since state must never be mutated directly (a rule covered when state is introduced). None of this is React-specific syntax; it's plain JavaScript you're learning now.

examples.title: Destructuring with Defaults and Renaming
examples.explanation: userName: user renames the userName property into a local variable called user rather than userName. role = "guest" is a default that doesn't apply here, since response.role exists ("admin"): defaults only kick in when the matched value is undefined. verified = false does apply, since response has no verified property at all, so destructuring that key gives undefined, and the default fills in. In the array example, secondary has no matching second element in ["red"], so its default "blue" is used.

examples.title: Spread for Merging, Rest for Collecting
examples.explanation: { ...defaults, ...overrides } copies defaults' properties first, then overrides' properties on top. Both objects have a timeout key, so overrides' value (8000) survives, because it's applied second and overwrites the earlier one. retries only exists on defaults, so it passes through unchanged. In logAll, label captures the first argument by position, and ...values, as a rest parameter, collects every remaining argument into a real array, so values.length, values.map(...), and every other array method work directly, unlike on the old arguments object.

misconceptions.description: Rest parameters (...rest) and the old arguments object are basically the same thing, just newer syntax.
misconceptions.clarification: A rest parameter produces a real Array -- it has map, filter, reduce, and every other array method directly available. arguments is only array-like: it has a length and numeric indices, but none of the array methods, so you'd have to convert it (e.g. Array.from(arguments)) before using them. Rest parameters also let you name the fixed leading parameters separately (function f(a, b, ...rest)), while arguments always contains every argument. Arrow functions have no arguments object of their own: inside an arrow function, arguments (if it resolves at all) refers to an enclosing non-arrow function's arguments, which is rarely what you want. Rest parameters work in every function form.

misconceptions.description: The ... syntax always does the same thing, whether you call it 'spread' or 'rest' -- the two names are just for different contexts of the identical behavior.
misconceptions.clarification: Spread and rest use the same three-dot syntax but perform opposite operations, and which one you get depends on where the ... appears. In an array/object literal or a function call's arguments, ... is spread: it expands an existing iterable/object into individual elements ([...arr], {...obj}, fn(...args)). In a function's parameter list (or at the end of a destructuring pattern), ... is rest: it collects the remaining values into one new array or object (function f(...rest)). Spread takes one thing apart into many; rest gathers many into one.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
hints: name: displayName renames a property. What value does it pull from user?
Defaults only apply when the matched value is undefined. Is user.email present but set to undefined, or missing entirely? Does that distinction matter?
age isn't a property on user at all, so what does destructuring a missing key give you before any default is applied?
exercises.expectedAnswer: Kofi no-email@example.com 30. displayName gets user.name via the rename; email's default applies because user.email is explicitly undefined (defaults trigger on undefined whether or not the key exists); age's default applies because the key is absent, which also reads as undefined.

Both cases follow the same rule (the default triggers on undefined), reached by two routes.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
hints: Object spread copies properties left to right -- when two spreads share a key, the one that appears later wins.
In merged1, adminOverrides is spread second -- what happens to role because of that?
merged2 spreads the same two objects in the opposite order. Does that change which role value survives?
exercises.expectedAnswer: merged1 is { role: 'admin', theme: 'light' } because adminOverrides is spread later and its role overwrites base's. merged2 is { role: 'viewer', theme: 'light' } because base is spread later this time, so its role overwrites adminOverrides'. Same two objects, opposite winner, because of spread order.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Object spread applies properties in the order the spreads appear, left to right, with later spreads overwriting earlier ones for any shared key. merged1 spreads base first (role: "viewer", theme: "light"), then adminOverrides second, so adminOverrides' role: "admin" overwrites the earlier viewer value, leaving { role: "admin", theme: "light" }. merged2 reverses the order (adminOverrides first, base second), so base's role: "viewer" is applied last and overwrites admin, giving { role: "viewer", theme: "light" }. When merging objects with spread, order matters: spread the more specific or more important object last.

options: A TypeError, because rest parameters can't be combined with a named parameter like name
"Rex: loyal, fast, loud" -- traits is an array-like arguments object, not a true Array
"Rex: [object Object]" -- traits is a plain object keyed by index
"Rex: loyal, fast, loud" -- traits is a real Array
assessments.explanation: name captures the first argument ("Rex") by position, and ...traits, as a rest parameter, collects every remaining argument ("loyal", "fast", "loud") into a real Array, which is why .join(", ") works directly on it, giving "Rex: loyal, fast, loud". Rest parameters combine with preceding named parameters (that's their normal use); they just can't have anything after them in the parameter list. The “"Rex: loyal, fast, loud" -- traits is an…” option describes the old arguments object, not a rest parameter; a rest parameter is a true array from the start, with no conversion needed.

assessments.prompt: A learner asks: "spread and rest both use ..., so aren't they the same feature?" Explain the difference, using one example of each.
assessments.modelAnswer: Spread and rest share the same syntax (...) but do opposite things, and which one applies depends on where the ... appears, not on any different keyword. Spread expands an existing collection out into individual elements, and it shows up inside array literals, object literals, or function call arguments: [...oldArray, newItem] takes oldArray apart into its individual elements and places them into a new array literal alongside newItem; Math.max(...numbers) takes an array apart into separate arguments to hand to a function that expects them individually rather than as one array. Rest does the reverse: it gathers individual values into a single new array, and it appears in a function's parameter list (or at the end of a destructuring pattern): function sum(...nums) { ... } called as sum(1, 2, 3) collects 1, 2, and 3 into one array bound to nums inside the function body. To tell them apart: if ... unpacks something that already exists into pieces, it's spread; if it packs separate incoming pieces into something new, it's rest.

concepts.title: map, filter, and reduce
concepts.description: map transforms every element into a new array of the same length, filter keeps only the elements that pass a test, and reduce folds an entire array down into a single value. Together they replace most manual for-loops over arrays.
learningObjectives: Use map to transform every element of an array into a new array of the same length.
Use filter to produce a new array containing only the elements that pass a predicate.
Trace reduce's accumulator step by step across an array to predict its final result.
Explain why reduce throws on an empty array with no initial value, and how to avoid it.
Chain map, filter, and reduce together to express a multi-step transformation declaratively.
Explain why these methods are generally preferred over manually written for-loops in modern JavaScript.

sections.heading: map: Transform Every Element
sections.body:
`array.map(callback)` calls `callback` once for every element and builds a **new array** out of whatever each call returns -- the result always has the same length as the original, one output for every input, and the original array is left untouched:

```javascript
const prices = [10, 20, 30];
const withMarkup = prices.map(price => price * 1.25);
console.log(withMarkup);   // [12.5, 25, 37.5]
console.log(prices);       // [10, 20, 30], unchanged
```

map is the tool for '**I have N things and I want N transformed things**.' The callback also receives the index as a second argument, `arr.map((item, i) => ...)`, which is handy for numbering items. If you find yourself calling `.map()` and never using the array it returns, for instance purely to trigger a side effect like a `console.log` in each callback, you want `.forEach()` instead (it returns `undefined` and builds nothing). Discarding a map's return value wastes what map is for.

sections.heading: filter: Keep Some Elements
sections.body:
`array.filter(predicate)` calls `predicate` once per element and builds a new array containing only the elements for which `predicate` returned a truthy value. The result can be shorter than the original (or the same length, or empty), and the original array is never mutated:

```javascript
const orders = [12, 45, 3, 88, 0, 21];
const nonZero = orders.filter(amount => amount > 0);
console.log(nonZero);   // [12, 45, 3, 88, 21]
```

filter is the tool for '**I have N things and I want just the ones matching some condition**.' The callback should return a boolean-ish value. Returning the element itself instead of a comparison is a common beginner mistake that works for truthy elements but drops every falsy one, including a legitimate `0` or `""` you wanted to keep.

sections.heading: reduce: Folding to a Single Value
sections.body:
`array.reduce(callback, initialValue)` is the one most people find hardest, because unlike map/filter it doesn't produce one output per input: it folds the **whole array down into a single value**, by calling `callback(accumulator, currentElement)` once per element and carrying the return value forward as the accumulator for the next call. Trace it step by step for `[10, 20, 30].reduce((acc, x) => acc + x, 0)`:

- Start: `acc = 0` (the `initialValue` you passed in)
- Element `10`: `callback(0, 10)` returns `10`, so `acc = 10`
- Element `20`: `callback(10, 20)` returns `30`, so `acc = 30`
- Element `30`: `callback(30, 30)` returns `60`, so `acc = 60`
- No more elements: `reduce` returns the final `acc`, `60`

The accumulator can be **any type**, not just a number: reducing into an object, a string, or another array is common (building a frequency count as `{ apple: 2, pear: 1 }`, or assembling a string from parts). The gotcha: **`initialValue` is optional, but skipping it changes the behavior**. If you omit it, `reduce` uses the array's *first element* as the starting accumulator and begins calling the callback from the *second* element instead of the first. For a non-empty array this can be fine, but for an **empty array with no `initialValue`**, there's nothing to use as a starting accumulator and no elements to iterate, so `reduce` throws `TypeError: Reduce of empty array with no initial value`. Pass an explicit `initialValue` unless you have a reason not to; it also removes the 'this works until someone passes an empty array' class of bugs.

sections.heading: Why Prefer These Over Manual Loops
sections.body: A hand-written `for` loop can do everything map/filter/reduce do, so the reason to prefer the array methods isn't capability. It's **readability and safety**. `array.map(x => x * 2)` states its intent in its name: 'transform each element.' A `for` loop doing the same thing makes you declare an index variable, declare and push into a results array, write the loop bound, and increment: four extra moving parts, each a place for an off-by-one error, a forgotten `push`, or a reused index variable to hide. The array methods also can't skip or double-count elements the way a hand-rolled loop with a wrong `<=` instead of `<` can. This is not a performance argument (a hand-written loop is occasionally slightly faster, and that rarely matters in application code). `.map()`, `.filter()`, and `.reduce()` each do one well-defined, well-named thing, so code that uses them is faster to read and trust than an equivalent loop whose purpose you have to reconstruct from its body.

sections.heading: Chaining Them Together
sections.body:
Because map and filter each return a new array, their results can be chained directly, letting you express a multi-step pipeline as one expression instead of several intermediate variables:

```javascript
const orders = [
  { item: "Book", price: 15, active: true },
  { item: "Pen", price: 2, active: false },
  { item: "Laptop", price: 999, active: true }
];

const activeTotal = orders
  .filter(order => order.active)
  .map(order => order.price)
  .reduce((sum, price) => sum + price, 0);

console.log(activeTotal);   // 1014
```

Each stage does one job: filter narrows down to active orders, map extracts the price from each, reduce folds those prices into a total. One caution: chaining is a readability tool, not a goal. A chain of five or six steps, or one with a deeply nested callback in the middle, can be harder to follow than a couple of clearly named intermediate variables. Chain as far as it stays easy to read at a glance.

examples.title: Tracing reduce Step by Step
examples.explanation: The initialValue 0 becomes sum on the first call, before any element has been processed. Each call's return value (sum + item.price) becomes the sum argument of the next call, which is what makes it an accumulator rather than a fresh variable each time. The trace shows sum starting at 0, becoming 15 after Book and 17 after Pen, and the last return value, 25, is what reduce returns once no elements are left.

examples.title: reduce Building an Object, Not a Number
examples.explanation: The accumulator here is an object ({}), not a number: reduce places no restriction on its type, it's whatever the callback returns each time. tally[vote] || 0 handles the first time a vote appears, when tally[vote] is undefined (falsy, so the || fallback supplies 0). Every call returns the same tally object (mutated in place), which carries the running counts forward. By the end, every distinct vote is a key in counts, with its value being how many times it appeared. This is a common reduce pattern beyond simple summing.

misconceptions.description: reduce's accumulator always has to be a number, since it usually shows up in summing examples.
misconceptions.clarification: The accumulator can be any value (an object, an array, a string, a boolean), and whatever the callback returns on each call becomes the next accumulator. Building a frequency-count object, flattening an array of arrays, or assembling a formatted string are common reduce patterns that never use a number as the accumulator.
misconceptions.fact: The accumulator can be any value (an object, an array, a string, a boolean), and whatever the callback returns on each call becomes the next accumulator.

misconceptions.description: map and forEach are basically interchangeable -- both just 'do something for every element.'
misconceptions.clarification: map returns a new array built from each callback's return value, and is meant to be used when you want that resulting array. forEach calls the callback for every element too, but always returns undefined; it makes no promise to collect anything. Writing const doubled = arr.forEach(x => x * 2) is a common bug: doubled ends up undefined, not an array of doubled values, because forEach discards what the callback returns. If you intend to use the returned array, use map; if you're only running a side effect (like logging), use forEach or a plain for...of loop.
misconceptions.fact: map returns a new array built from each callback's return value, and is meant to be used when you want that resulting array. forEach calls the callback for every element too, but always returns undefined; it makes no promise to collect anything.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and what is the value of total at the very end? Trace the accumulator through each call.
hints: No initialValue was passed here. Look at what reduce does differently in that case.
Without an initialValue, reduce uses the array's first element as the starting accumulator, and begins calling the callback from the second element onward.
So the first callback call here is acc=4 (the first element, used as the starting point) and n=9, not acc=undefined or some default.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 72. Since no initialValue is given, acc starts as nums[0] (4), and the callback runs starting from nums[1]: acc=4, n=9 gives 36; acc=36, n=2 gives 72. Only two callback calls happen, not three.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Because initialValue is omitted, reduce doesn't start with acc=0 or acc=undefined. It uses the array's first element, 4, as the starting accumulator and only calls the callback for the remaining elements: first for n=9 (acc * n = 4 * 9 = 36, becoming the new acc), then for n=2 (36 * 2 = 72, the final value). There are only two callback invocations for a three-element array in this no-initialValue mode, versus three if 1 had been passed as the initialValue (which also gives 72 here, since multiplying by 1 changes nothing; for other operations, or an empty array, omitting initialValue gives a different or invalid result, which is why being explicit is the safer habit).

exercises.prompt: This code is supposed to build an array of just the even numbers, doubled, but doubled ends up undefined instead of an array. Find and fix the bug.
hints: filter correctly narrows numbers down to the even ones; the bug is in what happens after that.
forEach calls its callback for every element, as map does, but does it do anything with what the callback returns?
Which array method collects each callback's return value into a new array?
exercises.solutionExplanation: filter(n => n % 2 === 0) correctly produces [2, 4, 6], the even numbers. The bug is the chained .forEach(n => n * 2): forEach calls its callback once per element (so n * 2 is computed three times), but it always returns undefined whatever the callback returns, and never collects anything into a new array. Swapping .forEach() for .map() fixes it, since map builds and returns a new array from each callback's return value, giving [4, 8, 12] as doubled.

exercises.prompt: Write a function `frequencyCount(words)` that takes an array of strings and returns an object mapping each distinct word to how many times it appears in the array, using reduce (not a manual for-loop). For example, frequencyCount(["a", "b", "a", "c", "b", "a"]) should return { a: 3, b: 2, c: 1 }.
hints: The accumulator doesn't have to be a number. What if it's an object that you build up across every element?
For each word, you need to know its current count so far (which is 0 if this is the first time you've seen it) and add one to it.
Pass an initial value to reduce, an empty object {}, and return the accumulator from every callback call so it carries forward.
exercises.solutionExplanation: reduce is called with an initial accumulator of {} (an empty object), which becomes counts on the first call. For each word, counts[word] || 0 reads the running total so far: 0 the first time a word is seen, since counts[word] is undefined and therefore falsy, and the real count on later occurrences. Adding 1 gives the new count for that word. Returning counts from every callback call is essential: the accumulator is what gets passed to the next call, so forgetting to return it would make the next call receive undefined as counts and throw when reading counts[word].

assessments.prompt:
```javascript
const result = [].reduce((acc, x) => acc + x);
```
What happens when this line runs?
options: result becomes 0
It throws a TypeError
result becomes undefined
result becomes NaN
assessments.explanation: With no initialValue supplied, reduce falls back to the array's first element as the starting accumulator, but this array is empty, so there is no first element and nothing to iterate over. Instead of producing a default value, reduce throws TypeError: Reduce of empty array with no initial value. This is why passing an explicit initialValue is the safer habit: [].reduce((acc, x) => acc + x, 0) returns 0 instead of throwing, since there's a defined starting point even with zero elements.

assessments.prompt: A teammate has a for loop that builds an array of formatted display names from a list of user objects, skipping any user marked as deleted. They ask whether it's worth rewriting it with filter and map. Give your recommendation and explain the trade-offs.
assessments.modelAnswer: Yes, this is close to the ideal case for filter/map: two well-defined steps, 'keep only non-deleted users' and 'transform each remaining user into a display name', map onto filter(user => !user.deleted).map(user => formatName(user)). The rewrite states each step's intent in its name, so a reader can understand the code without simulating the loop body, and it removes the manual bookkeeping (an index variable, a results array to push into, remembering to skip deleted users) where off-by-one or forgotten-push bugs tend to hide. Trade-offs: performance is not a reason to switch either way for ordinary list sizes (a for loop is occasionally slightly faster, which rarely matters for UI-scale data), so this is a readability decision, not an optimization. Also check whether the original loop does more than filter and transform: if it needs to break out early, or track an index or running total while building the array, a plain filter().map() chain may not capture everything, and forcing that shape could make the code more convoluted. For the case described, a straightforward filter-then-transform, filter/map is a clear improvement.

concepts.title: Modules
concepts.description: ES Modules let you split code across files with import/export, giving each file its own private scope by default and a choice between one default export and any number of named exports.
learningObjectives: Write and use both named exports/imports and a default export/import.
Explain the practical difference between default and named exports, and when to prefer named exports.
Explain that each module has its own top-level scope, and nothing leaks out of it unless explicitly exported.
Recognize that Node's older CommonJS (require/module.exports) system is a different, incompatible syntax for a similar idea.

sections.heading: Named Exports vs Default Exports
sections.body: A module can export values in two ways. A **named export** exposes a value under a specific name: `export const PI = 3.14159;` or `export function formatDate(d) { ... }`. Importing it requires matching that exact name inside curly braces: `import { PI, formatDate } from "./constants.js";`. A module can have **any number** of named exports. A **default export** exposes a single, primary value with no fixed name attached to it at the export site: `export default function formatDate(d) { ... }`. Importing it uses no curly braces, and **the importer chooses the local name**: `import myDateFormatter from "./formatDate.js";` works the same as `import formatDate from "./formatDate.js";`, since the name is up to the import statement, not fixed by the export. That is the key structural difference. A module can have **at most one** default export. (In Node, files using this syntax need a `.mjs` extension or `"type": "module"` in `package.json`; bundlers and browsers loading `<script type="module">` handle it directly.)

sections.heading: When to Prefer Named Exports
sections.body: Modern JavaScript style generally favors named exports over default exports, for a practical reason: **refactor safety**. A named export's name is fixed, so every import of it must use that name (or alias it with `as`). Tooling such as your editor's rename-symbol feature, a find-all-references search, or an automated codemod can then track every usage across a codebase and update them together. A default export has no such anchor: every importer can name it anything, so two files importing the same default export might call it two different things, and neither a tool nor a person skimming the code can tell they're the same thing from the name. This isn't a hard rule. Default exports are still common for a module whose purpose is one thing (a single React component file is a frequent example). But 'named by default, default export only when there's one obvious thing to export' is the pragmatic guideline, because it keeps large codebases easier to navigate and rename safely.

sections.heading: Module Scope
sections.body: Every module (every file, when using this syntax) has its **own top-level scope**: a variable, function, or class declared at the top level of one file is private to that file, invisible to every other file, unless it's exported. This improves on the old plain-`<script>`-tag era, where every script on a page shared one global scope, and a top-level `var` or `function` in one script could overwrite an identically named one from another script, depending on load order. With modules, `const helper = () => {...}` in `fileA.js` and an unrelated `const helper = () => {...}` in `fileB.js` never conflict: neither is visible outside its own file unless exported, so there's no global namespace for them to collide in.

sections.heading: A Note on CommonJS
sections.body: If you look at older Node.js code (or some npm packages, especially ones written some years ago), you'll see a different, older module syntax: `const fs = require("fs");` for importing, and `module.exports = myFunction;` or `exports.myFunction = myFunction;` for exporting. This is **CommonJS**, Node's original module system. It predates native support for ES Modules (the `import`/`export` syntax covered here) in both Node and browsers. The two systems are not interchangeable syntax for the same thing. CommonJS loads modules synchronously and resolves them when `require` runs; ES Modules are statically analyzable and support features CommonJS doesn't, like live bindings and top-level await. You don't need those details yet. What matters now is recognition: if you see `require(...)` in a file, it's using CommonJS, not the `import`/`export` syntax this concept covers, and mixing the two carelessly in one project is a common source of confusing errors.

examples.title: Named Exports and Imports
examples.explanation: mathUtils.js exports two named bindings, PI and circleArea, each with a fixed name attached at the export site. app.js imports both by matching those names inside curly braces. If either name were misspelled, the import would fail with a SyntaxError, since named imports must match exactly (or be renamed with as). A module can have any number of named exports; the one-per-module limit applies only to default exports.

examples.title: A Default Export, Imported Under Any Name
examples.explanation: formatCurrency.js has one default export, an anonymous function (default exports don't need a name at the export site). Both fileA.js and fileB.js import that same default export, but each chooses its own local name (formatCurrency in one, money in the other). Neither choice is wrong, and nothing in the names shows they refer to the same function. That is the flexibility, and the refactor-safety downside, that named exports don't have.

misconceptions.description: A module can have multiple default exports, the same way it can have multiple named exports.
misconceptions.clarification: A module can have at most one default export; a second export default in the same file is a SyntaxError. Named exports have no such limit; you can export as many named values as you like from one module. If a module needs to expose several equally important things, use named exports, not multiple defaults (impossible) or one default object holding everything (possible, but it loses most of the refactor-safety benefit of named exports).
misconceptions.fact: A module can have at most one default export; a second export default in the same file is a SyntaxError.

misconceptions.description: A variable or function declared at the top level of a module file is global, just like it would be in a plain <script> tag.
misconceptions.clarification: Each module has its own private top-level scope. A top-level const, function, or class in one file is invisible to every other file unless it's explicitly exported with the export keyword, and even then, another file must import it to use it. This differs from the old plain-<script>-tag model, where every loaded script shared one global scope and same-named top-level declarations in different scripts could collide.
misconceptions.fact: Each module has its own private top-level scope.

exercises.prompt: Given these two files, what happens when app.js runs?
hints: Look at which function is the default export and which is a named export. The import statement in app.js has them backwards.
Named exports must be imported inside curly braces using their exact fixed name; a default export is imported with no curly braces, under any name you choose.
shout was exported as a named export, but app.js imports it as if it were the default, and asks for a named export called whisper. Does the module provide that?
exercises.expectedAnswer: Nothing prints. The import fails before any code in app.js runs, with a SyntaxError saying the module does not provide an export named 'whisper' (the only named export is shout; whisper is the default export). The import statement has the two export styles swapped.
exercises.solutionExplanation: stringUtils.js exports shout as a named export and whisper as the default export, the opposite of how app.js imports them. import shout, { whisper } from ... binds the local name shout to the module's default export (the whisper function) and asks for a named export literally called whisper, which doesn't exist. In native ES modules that mismatch is caught while the module graph is linked, so app.js never runs and nothing is logged. (Some bundlers are more lenient: shout("hello") would then run whisper's logic and print "hello...", and whisper would be undefined.) The fix is to match each import to its actual export style: import { shout } from ... for the named export, and import whisper from ... (or any name) for the default.

exercises.prompt: This code throws a SyntaxError about a duplicate default export. Find the problem and fix it using named exports instead.
hints: How many default exports is a single module allowed to have?
config.js exports two configuration objects, both as defaults, which isn't allowed.
Named exports don't have this one-per-module limit -- can you give each object its own fixed name instead?
exercises.solutionExplanation: A module can have at most one export default. config.js declares two, which is a SyntaxError caught before the module runs, not a runtime error.
