Since there are two separate, equally important values to expose, named exports are the right tool: each configuration object gets its own exported name (retryConfig, timeoutConfig), and app.js imports both by name inside curly braces. This also avoids the ambiguity of a single combined default object, where callers would need to know to write settings.retries and settings.timeout.

assessments.prompt: Why do many style guides prefer named exports over default exports for most modules?
options: Default exports are not supported in Node.js, only in browsers.
Named exports run faster at import time than default exports.
Named exports have a fixed name enforced at every import site.
A module can only have one named export, so named exports are simpler to reason about.
assessments.explanation: The practical reason is refactor safety: a named export's name is fixed, so every import of it must match (or alias it), which lets an editor's rename tool or a find-all-references search catch every usage. A default export can be imported under any local name the importer chooses, so two files importing the 'same' default export might call it two different things, with nothing to connect them. Performance (“Named exports run faster at import time…”) isn't a factor here. The “Default exports are not supported in Node.js…” option is false: default exports work the same in Node and browsers. The “A module can only have one named…” option has the limit backwards: default exports are capped at one per module, not named exports.

assessments.prompt: Explain why declaring `const cache = {}` at the top of one module file doesn't create a global variable accessible from other files, and contrast this with how top-level variables worked in plain <script>-tag JavaScript.
assessments.modelAnswer: Each module (each file using import/export syntax) gets its own private top-level scope, separate from every other module's. A const declared at the top level of one file lives only in that file's module scope; it is never automatically visible elsewhere, however many other files are loaded into the same page or program. Another file can see it only if the original module exports it (export const cache = {}) and the other file imports it (import { cache } from "./thatFile.js"). This is a deliberate change from the older plain-<script>-tag model, where every script tag on a page shared one global scope, so a top-level var or function in one script became visible to (and could be overwritten by) any other script on the page, depending on load order, with no opt-in. Module scope removes that kind of accidental cross-file collision: nothing leaks between files unless a developer exports and imports it, which makes large codebases easier to reason about.

concepts.title: The DOM and Events
concepts.description: The DOM is a live, mutable tree of objects representing the current page, not the original HTML text. querySelector, addEventListener, and event bubbling are the manual tools that React's JSX and synthetic event system abstract away.
learningObjectives: Explain that the DOM is a live tree of objects representing the current page, distinct from the original HTML source text.
Select and mutate elements directly using querySelector and standard DOM properties.
Attach event listeners with addEventListener and explain why removeEventListener requires the same function reference.
Explain event bubbling at a conceptual level and predict the order handlers fire in a nested click.
Explain what React's JSX and synthetic event system abstract away, and why that context makes React's behavior less 'magic.'

sections.heading: The DOM Is a Live Tree of Objects
sections.body: The **DOM** (Document Object Model) is the browser's in-memory representation of the current page: a tree of JavaScript objects (`Node`s -- elements, text, comments), each with properties and methods, mirroring the nested structure of the HTML. **The DOM is not the HTML source text.** It's a live, mutable data structure that the browser builds by parsing that text once, and that JavaScript can then read and change, with the visible page updating immediately to match. After some JavaScript has run, 'view source' (the raw HTML the server sent) and the browser DevTools Elements panel (the live DOM) can look completely different: DevTools shows the DOM as it exists *right now*, including anything JavaScript has added, removed, or changed since the page loaded, while 'view source' shows only the original text. Every `document.createElement`, every `.textContent = ...` assignment, and every `.appendChild(...)` call mutates this live tree, not some underlying text file.

sections.heading: Selecting and Mutating Elements
sections.body: `document.querySelector(cssSelector)` returns the first element matching a CSS selector (`document.querySelector("#submit-btn")`, `document.querySelector(".card.active")`), or `null` if nothing matches; `document.querySelectorAll(cssSelector)` returns all matches as a `NodeList`. Once you have a reference to an element, you mutate it through its properties: `el.textContent = "Updated"` sets its text safely; `el.classList.add("active")` / `.remove(...)` / `.toggle(...)` manage CSS classes without parsing or rebuilding a class string; `el.style.color = "red"` sets an inline style. A safety note: `el.innerHTML = someString` parses `someString` as HTML and inserts it, so if it contains unsanitized user input you've opened a cross-site-scripting (XSS) hole. `

sections.heading: Attaching Event Listeners
sections.body: `el.addEventListener("click", handlerFunction)` registers `handlerFunction` to run whenever a `click` event fires on `el`. Unlike the old single-slot `el.onclick = fn` approach, `addEventListener` lets you attach **multiple independent listeners** for the same event type to the same element -- all of them run, in the order they were added. To remove one later, `el.removeEventListener("click", handlerFunction)` requires passing **the exact same function reference** that was originally added -- calling `removeEventListener` with a new arrow function or anonymous function, even one with identical code, removes nothing, because it's a different function value that was never registered. This is why code that needs to remove a listener later stores the handler in a named variable or constant first, rather than passing an inline anonymous function to `addEventListener`. (For a handler that should run only once, pass `{ once: true }` as the third argument and the browser removes it for you.)

sections.heading: Event Bubbling
sections.body: When an event fires on an element, it doesn't only run listeners attached to that element. By default it then **bubbles up** through the element's ancestors, running matching listeners on each in turn, all the way up to `document`. Clicking a button nested inside several `<div>`s fires the button's own click listener first, then the enclosing div's (if it has one), then that div's parent's, and so on outward. This outward propagation is what makes **event delegation** possible: instead of attaching a listener to every item in a long list, you attach one listener to the list's parent and inspect `event.target` (the element actually clicked), letting bubbling deliver every child click to that listener. It's also why `event.stopPropagation()` exists: it stops an event from bubbling further when a handler should be the last to react.

sections.heading: Why This Matters for React
sections.body: React abstracts almost all of the above away, and knowing what's underneath turns React's behavior from magic into something that makes sense. You never call `document.createElement` or `.appendChild` yourself in React code: JSX (covered in the React Fundamentals module) compiles to element descriptions that React turns into real DOM nodes, using the same DOM APIs covered here, automated. You don't typically call `addEventListener` directly either. Writing `<button onClick={handleClick}>` in JSX is React's declarative equivalent, wired up through React's own **synthetic event system**, a layer on top of real DOM events that normalizes inconsistencies across browsers (React also batches the state updates a handler makes). Synthetic events still bubble the way real DOM events do: a `stopPropagation()` call on a React synthetic event stops it from reaching a React `onClick` on a parent component, for the same reason a real listener's `stopPropagation()` does. It's the same tree, the same events, the same bubbling, wrapped in a more declarative API.

examples.title: Selecting, Mutating, and Listening
examples.explanation: querySelector finds the live button element on the page, the same object the browser uses to render what's on screen, not a copy or a description of it. Each click mutates that element: textContent updates the visible label immediately, and classList.toggle flips the active class, which the page's CSS presumably uses to change the button's appearance. handleClick is a named function so that a later removeEventListener call can reference the identical function value; a freshly written function expression, even with identical code, would fail to remove anything, since it wouldn't match the reference addEventListener stored.

examples.title: Event Bubbling Order
examples.explanation: Clicking the button fires the click event on the button first, since it's the target of the click, so "button" logs first. The event then bubbles outward, reaching #inner (the button's parent) and logging "inner", and finally #outer, logging "outer". No listener calls stopPropagation(), so the event keeps bubbling through every ancestor with a matching listener, firing each in inside-to-outside order.

misconceptions.description: The DOM is just the HTML source code, so inspecting an element in DevTools shows you exactly what's in the original HTML file.
misconceptions.clarification: The DOM is a live, in-memory tree of objects that the browser builds by parsing the HTML once, and JavaScript can then read and mutate that tree directly; the visible page reflects the DOM's current state, not the original source text. DevTools' Elements panel shows the DOM as it exists right now, including any changes JavaScript has made since the page loaded; 'view page source' shows only the original HTML the server sent. After enough JavaScript has run, the two can look completely different.
misconceptions.fact: The DOM is a live, in-memory tree of objects that the browser builds by parsing the HTML once, and JavaScript can then read and mutate that tree directly; the visible page reflects the DOM's current state, not the original source text.

misconceptions.description: Calling el.removeEventListener("click", function() { ... }) removes a listener as long as the function's code looks the same as what was originally passed to addEventListener.
misconceptions.clarification: removeEventListener only removes a listener if it's given the exact same function reference that was originally passed to addEventListener ; it compares by identity, not by what the function's code does or looks like. Two separately written functions with identical bodies are still two different function values in memory, so passing a freshly written one to removeEventListener does nothing (no error; the old listener stays attached). To be able to remove a listener later, store the handler in a named variable/constant and pass that same reference to both addEventListener and removeEventListener.
misconceptions.fact: removeEventListener only removes a listener if it's given the exact same function reference that was originally passed to addEventListener ; it compares by identity, not by what the function's code does or looks like.

exercises.prompt:
Given `
New
`, and this code, what gets logged, in what order, when the user clicks directly on the badge span?
exercises.code:
document.querySelector("#card").addEventListener("click", () => console.log("card clicked"));
document.querySelector("#badge").addEventListener("click", () => console.log("badge clicked"));
hints: The click's target is the badge, since that's the element the user clicked. Which listener fires for that first?
After firing on its target, an event doesn't stop there by default. What does it do next, and in which direction through the tree?
card is badge's parent. Does the event reach card's listener before or after badge's?
exercises.expectedAnswer: "badge clicked" logs first, then "card clicked": the event fires on its target (badge) first, then bubbles upward to the parent (card).
exercises.solutionExplanation: The click event fires on its target first (the element the user clicked, #badge here), so "badge clicked" logs first. After the target, the event bubbles upward through each ancestor, and #card is badge's direct parent, so card's click listener fires next and logs "card clicked". Neither listener calls stopPropagation(), so nothing interrupts the bubbling.

exercises.prompt: This code is supposed to let the user toggle a highlight on and off by clicking a button repeatedly, and later remove that ability entirely by calling disableHighlighting(). But calling disableHighlighting() never actually removes the click behavior. Find and fix the bug.
hints: removeEventListener needs the same function reference that addEventListener received, not just similar-looking code.
Each of these two functions writes its own anonymous function() {...}. Are those two function expressions the same value in memory?
Try storing the handler in a named variable once, outside both functions, and passing that one reference to both addEventListener and removeEventListener.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code writes two anonymous function expressions, one inside enableHighlighting and one inside disableHighlighting, and although their code is identical, they are different function values in memory. removeEventListener compares by reference, not by code, so passing a function that was never registered does nothing, with no error. The fix pulls the handler out into a named function, toggleHighlight, declared once; both enableHighlighting and disableHighlighting reference that same function value, so removeEventListener can find and remove the listener that addEventListener added.

assessments.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between the DOM and the original HTML sent by the server?
options: The DOM is a live, mutable tree of objects built by parsing the HTML once.
innerHTML and textContent behave identically, since both just set an element's HTML content.
The DOM only updates when the page is reloaded from the server.
The DOM and the original HTML source are always identical -- inspecting either one shows the same content.
assessments.explanation: The DOM starts as a tree built by parsing the original HTML, but after that it's an independent, live, in-memory structure. JavaScript mutations to it (adding elements, changing text, updating attributes) take effect immediately on the visible page and don't touch or require re-fetching the original source. The “The DOM and the original HTML source…” option is false the moment any JavaScript runs and changes something. The “The DOM only updates when the page…” option is false: DOM updates happen immediately via script, with no reload needed. The “innerHTML and textContent behave identically, since both…” option is false, and dangerous to believe: innerHTML parses its argument as HTML markup (an XSS risk with untrusted input), while textContent always treats its argument as plain text.

assessments.prompt: A developer who has only used React is confused by a bug involving addEventListener and asks why React never made them think about event bubbling before. Explain what React normally abstracts away here, and why understanding real DOM events still matters.
assessments.modelAnswer: In plain JavaScript, you manually select real DOM elements (querySelector), manually attach listeners to them (addEventListener), and those events bubble upward through the actual DOM tree by default, which is the mechanism this concept covers. React abstracts almost every part of that away: JSX like <button onClick={handleClick}> leads React to create the DOM element and attach the event handling for you, so you never call addEventListener yourself in typical React code. React also layers its own synthetic event system on top of native browser events, mainly to smooth out cross-browser inconsistencies, so what a React onClick handler receives (event) is a React wrapper object, not the same object a raw addEventListener callback would get. (React also batches the state updates a handler triggers.) Native bubbling still matters because React's synthetic events bubble the way real DOM events do: a stopPropagation() call inside a React onClick can stop that click from triggering a parent component's onClick, for the same reason a real stopPropagation() would. Debugging a click on a nested element that also fires something on a parent, or working out why event delegation works in a component tree, comes back to the bubbling model covered here. React didn't replace that model, it wrapped it in a more declarative API, so the mental model transfers directly.

concepts.title: Promises and async/await
concepts.description: A Promise represents an eventual result that settles exactly once, async/await is syntactic sugar for working with promises using synchronous-looking code, and awaiting inside a loop is a common performance mistake in async code.
learningObjectives: Explain the readability and error-handling problems nested callbacks caused, and how promises address them.
Name a Promise's three states and explain what it means for a promise to settle exactly once.
Chain .then()/.catch() correctly and predict how errors propagate through a chain.
Explain that an async function always returns a promise, even when its body returns a plain value.
Identify when awaiting inside a loop unnecessarily serializes independent async work, and fix it with Promise.all.

sections.heading: The Callback Problem
A Promise's Three States
sections.body: A **Promise** is an object representing the eventual result of an asynchronous operation. Every promise is in exactly one of three states at any given moment: **pending** (the operation hasn't finished yet; the initial state of every promise), **fulfilled** (the operation completed successfully, and the promise now holds a resulting value), or **rejected** (the operation failed, and the promise now holds a reason/error). The key rule: a **promise settles exactly once**. Once it moves from pending to fulfilled or rejected, it is locked into that state and value/reason permanently. It can't change state later, resolve a second time with a different value, or flip between fulfilled and rejected. This is why a promise is a poor model for something that changes repeatedly over time (like a stream of events): it models a single, one-time outcome.

sections.heading: .then() and .catch() Chaining
sections.body:
`.then(onFulfilled, onRejected)` registers callbacks to run once a promise settles; `.catch(onRejected)` is shorthand for `.then(undefined, onRejected)`. What solves the nesting problem is that **`.then()` always returns a new promise**, so calls chain one after another instead of nesting:

```javascript
getUser(userId)
  .then(user => getPosts(user.id))
  .then(posts => getComments(posts[0].id))
  .then(comments => console.log(comments))
  .catch(err => console.error("Something failed:", err));
```

If any `.then()` callback returns a plain value, the next `.then()` in the chain receives that value directly. If a `.then()` callback instead returns *another promise* (as `getPosts(user.id)` does above), the chain waits for that inner promise to settle and 'flattens' it: the next `.then()` receives the eventual plain value, not a promise wrapping a promise. And a single `.catch()` at the end of the chain catches a rejection or a thrown error from **any** earlier step, one shared error handler for the whole sequence, which fixes callback hell's duplicated error handling. A common mistake in chains is forgetting to `return` the inner promise from a `.then()` callback: the chain then doesn't wait for it, and the next step receives `undefined`.

sections.heading: async/await as Sugar Over Promises
The Await-in-a-Loop Pitfall

examples.title: The Same Sequential Task: Callbacks vs Promises vs async/await
examples.explanation: All three versions do the same work in the same order: fetch a user, then that user's posts, then log them. The callback version nests one level deeper per step and needs handleError passed in at each level. The promise chain flattens the nesting into a linear .then() sequence with one shared .catch() at the end. The async/await version reads most like synchronous code, each await meaning 'wait here, then continue with the value', with one try/catch covering every awaited step, as you'd structure error handling in synchronous code. (The snippet assumes getUser, getPosts, and handleError exist.)

examples.title: async Functions Always Return a Promise
examples.explanation: double is declared async, so calling it never gives you x * 2 directly. It gives you a promise, and JavaScript wraps the returned value (10) into a fulfilled promise. console.log(result) shows the promise object, not the number. Getting the 10 out requires unwrapping the promise, with .then() (usable outside any async function) or with await inside another async function; both are two syntaxes for 'wait for this promise, then hand me its value'.

examples.title: await-in-a-Loop vs Promise.all
examples.explanation: loadSequential's for loop awaits each fetchUser call before moving to the next id, so the three requests run back to back, roughly 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 seconds, though none depends on another's result. loadConcurrent calls fetchUser for every id first, with no awaiting in between, so all three requests are in flight by the time Promise.all is reached; Promise.all then waits for the slowest, so the whole operation takes about as long as the slowest fetch, about 1 second, not 3. The results array from Promise.all keeps the original ids order regardless of which fetch finishes first.

misconceptions.description: await pauses all of JavaScript, blocking the entire page/program until the promise resolves.
misconceptions.clarification: await only pauses the execution of the specific async function it appears inside; it does not block the JavaScript engine's event loop or any other code. While one async function is paused at an await, other functions, event handlers, and already-scheduled work keep running. This is why await never freezes a page's UI the way a long-running synchronous loop would.
misconceptions.fact: await only pauses the execution of the specific async function it appears inside; it does not block the JavaScript engine's event loop or any other code.

misconceptions.description: An async function that does `return 5;` returns the plain number 5, since that's literally what the return statement says.
misconceptions.clarification: Every async function returns a Promise, whatever its return statement returns; the returned value is wrapped in a fulfilled promise. return 5; inside an async function produces a promise that fulfills with 5, not the number 5. Getting the plain 5 out requires unwrapping that promise, via await (inside another async function) or .then().

misconceptions.description: A promise can be resolved more than once, or you can .then() it repeatedly to get a fresh, updated value each time, similar to how an event listener fires repeatedly.
misconceptions.clarification: A promise settles exactly once: it transitions from pending to fulfilled or rejected a single time, permanently, and calling resolve or reject again afterward has no effect. Any number of .then() callbacks, registered before or after the promise settles, all receive that same final value (or none, if the promise never settles). A promise models a single outcome, not a repeating stream of values; for repeating async events, use something else, like an event listener or an observable/stream.
misconceptions.fact: A promise settles exactly once: it transitions from pending to fulfilled or rejected a single time, permanently, and calling resolve or reject again afterward has no effect.

exercises.prompt: In what order do these four lines log?
hints: Everything before the first await inside an async function runs synchronously, the moment the function is called.
The line right after foo() is called, console.log("D"), is ordinary synchronous code in the main flow of the script. Does it have to wait for foo to finish?

await always yields control back to the rest of the program at least once, even when awaiting something already resolved (like null). The code after await resumes only after the current synchronous code has finished.
exercises.expectedAnswer: A, B, D, C. foo() runs synchronously up through console.log("B") and then the await, where it pauses and control returns to the main script, which logs D; only after the main synchronous code finishes does foo() resume after its await, logging C last.
exercises.solutionExplanation: console.log("A") runs first, as ordinary top-level code. Calling foo() runs synchronously until it hits an await, so console.log("B") runs immediately as part of that call, before foo() returns to its caller. At await null, foo pauses and hands control back to its caller. null isn't even a pending promise, but await always defers its continuation to at least the next microtask and never resumes in the same synchronous pass. So execution returns to the line after foo(), console.log("D"), which runs next as plain synchronous code. Only when all currently running synchronous code (including that D log) has finished does the engine process the queued continuation of foo(), which resumes after the await and logs "C". This A, B, D, C ordering is a classic async/await gotcha, because await null looks like it should do nothing but still yields at least one turn.

exercises.prompt: This function fetches profile data for five independent user IDs, but it's slower than expected: each request seems to wait for the previous one. Find and fix the performance bug.
hints: fetchProfile(id) for one id doesn't depend on the result of fetchProfile for any other id, so the five requests are independent.
Inside the for loop, await pauses the loop before the next iteration, so no request starts until the previous one has finished.
Try starting every fetchProfile call first (with .map, no await yet), then waiting for all the resulting promises together.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original for loop awaits fetchProfile(id) on every iteration before moving to the next id, so each of the five requests waits for the previous one to finish before it starts. That turns five independent requests into a serial chain, roughly five times slower than necessary. The fix uses userIds.map(id => fetchProfile(id)) to call fetchProfile for every id immediately, with no awaiting in between, so all five requests are in flight before the function waits at all. await Promise.all(promises) then waits for all of them, resolving once the slowest finishes, and returns an array of results in the same order as userIds. The total time is about that of the slowest request, not the sum of all five.

exercises.prompt: Given an already-implemented function `fetchUser(id)` that returns a promise resolving to a user object, write an async function `loadUsersConcurrently(ids)` that fetches the users for all the given ids concurrently (not one at a time) and returns a promise resolving to an array of the user objects, in the same order as ids. If any individual fetch fails, the whole function should reject with that error.
hints: Kick off every fetchUser call first, with no await yet, so all the requests start at roughly the same time.
.map over ids to get back an array of promises: one call per id, none awaited individually.

Promise.all takes an array of promises and returns one promise that resolves with an array of all their results, in the same order. It rejects if any one of them rejects, which matches the required behavior.
exercises.solutionExplanation: ids.map(id => fetchUser(id)) calls fetchUser once per id, immediately and with no awaiting in between, so every request starts at about the same time, which satisfies the concurrency requirement. Promise.all(promises) takes that array of in-flight promises and returns a new promise that resolves once all of them have resolved, with an array of their results in the order the promises were given (regardless of which finishes first), which satisfies the 'same order as ids' requirement. Promise.all also rejects as soon as any promise in the array rejects, which is the required 'reject with that error if any fetch fails' behavior, with no extra code.

options: "Amara"
A Promise object (which will fulfill with the value "Amara")
undefined
A SyntaxError, since async functions can't return plain strings
assessments.explanation: Every async function returns a promise, whatever its return statement returns: the value "Amara" is wrapped into a promise that fulfills with it. Calling getName() without awaiting or .then()-ing it gives you the promise object, not the eventual string. Getting "Amara" out requires await getName() inside another async function, or getName().then(name => ...). Returning a plain string from an async function is fine and common; it's just wrapped implicitly.

assessments.prompt: A colleague's code fetches five independent pieces of data using five separate awaited calls inside a for loop, and complains that the page feels sluggish. Explain what's likely happening and how you'd fix it, including any caveat about the fix.
assessments.modelAnswer: The likely problem is the await-in-a-loop pattern: if the loop awaits each async call before the next iteration, the five requests, though none depends on another's result, run one after another instead of at the same time. If each takes half a second, that's about two and a half seconds instead of about half a second, which fits a 'sluggish' complaint. The fix is to stop awaiting inside the loop and start every request immediately (commonly via .map(id => someAsyncCall(id)), which collects the promises into an array), then await Promise.all(thatArray) once, outside the loop. One caveat to raise with the colleague: Promise.all rejects as soon as any one of the five requests fails, discarding the results of any that already succeeded. If the use case needs the outcome of every request regardless of individual failures (say, 'show whichever of these five succeeded, and flag which ones failed'), Promise.allSettled is the better tool, since it resolves with a per-item status instead of rejecting the batch on the first failure.

concepts.title: fetch and Error Handling
concepts.description: The fetch API's promise resolves for any completed HTTP response, including 404s and 500s, and rejects only on network-level failure, so you must check response.ok yourself. Missing this is a common mistake that leads to swallowed errors.
learningObjectives: Describe the basic shape of a fetch call, including the separate step needed to read the response body.
Explain that fetch's promise rejects only on network failure, not on HTTP error status codes, and check response.ok/response.status accordingly.
Write a fetch call wrapped in try/catch using async/await that correctly handles both network failures and HTTP error responses.
Explain how the loading/success/error pattern shown here maps onto how React data-fetching hooks are typically built.

sections.heading: The fetch API's Basic Shape
fetch Does Not Throw on HTTP Error Status Codes
sections.body:
This is the most common and most costly misconception about `fetch`: **its promise does not reject just because the server responded with an error status like 404 or 500.** To `fetch`, a 404 Not Found is a *completed HTTP exchange*: the server responded, the browser got a full response, and the network transport didn't fail. So the promise **resolves** normally, with a `Response` object whose `.status` is `404`. The promise only **rejects** for network-level failures: DNS resolution failure, no connectivity at all, a CORS policy blocking the request, the connection being dropped mid-flight.

So code like `fetch(url).then(res => res.json()).catch(err => handleError(err))` proceeds past `.then()` and never reaches `.catch()` even when the server returns a 500 with an error body. It hands you the parsed error JSON as if it were a normal result, with nothing signaling that anything went wrong. You must check **`response.ok`** (a boolean, `true` for any status in the 200-299 range) or **`response.status`** yourself and decide what 'failure' means for your case, typically by throwing an error when `response.ok` is `false`, so that your existing error-handling path (`.catch()` or `try`/`catch`) gets a chance to run.

sections.heading: try/catch with async/await
This Pattern Is What React Data-Fetching Hooks Are Built Around
sections.body: React's data-fetching patterns are built on a three-state model: **loading** (the request is in flight), **success** (data arrived), and **error** (something went wrong, whether at the network level or an HTTP error status you detected). A typical custom hook for fetching data (`useEffect` plus a few `useState` calls, or a library like React Query/TanStack Query) runs the same `try`/`await fetch`/check-`response.ok`/`catch` logic shown here and exposes its outcome as those three states (`isLoading`, `data`, `error`) for a component to render conditionally. Knowing the plain-JavaScript version first makes those hooks predictable rather than opaque: the same pattern is inside them, wrapped in React's state and lifecycle management.

examples.title: Basic fetch with async/await
examples.explanation: The first await waits for the HTTP response to arrive and gives back a Response object. Headers and status are available at that point, but the body hasn't been read yet. The second await, on response.json(), waits for the body to be read and parsed as JSON, a separate asynchronous step. The example omits error handling to show the two-step shape; the next example shows why that omission is dangerous.

examples.title: The Misconception in Action: A 404 That Never Reaches catch
examples.explanation: In the first version, fetch's promise resolves normally for the 404 response: as far as fetch is concerned, the request completed, and it happens to carry a 404 status. res.json() also resolves, parsing whatever error body the server sent (perhaps { error: "User not found" }), and the second .then() logs it as if it were a successful result. .catch() never runs, because nothing in the chain rejected. The fixed version adds a res.ok check inside the first .then() and throws an Error when it's false. Throwing inside a .then() callback rejects the chain from that point on, which gives .catch() something to catch.

misconceptions.description: fetch automatically throws an error (or rejects its promise) whenever the server responds with an error status like 404 or 500.
misconceptions.clarification: fetch's promise only rejects for network-level failures: no connectivity, DNS failure, a blocked CORS request, a dropped connection. A completed HTTP exchange that happens to carry a 404 or 500 status is, from fetch's point of view, a completed request/response cycle, so the promise resolves with a Response object whose status/ok properties reflect the error. You must check response.ok (or response.status) and decide what counts as a failure for your use case, typically by throwing your own Error when it's not ok, so your catch block or .catch() gets triggered.
misconceptions.fact: fetch's promise only rejects for network-level failures: no connectivity, DNS failure, a blocked CORS request, a dropped connection.

misconceptions.description: Once you have the Response object from fetch, you already have the actual data -- it's already been parsed and is ready to use.
misconceptions.clarification: The Response object gives you access to metadata (status, headers, ok) as soon as the response starts arriving, but reading and parsing the body is a separate asynchronous step: response.json() (or .text(), .blob(), etc.) returns another promise that needs its own await or .then(). The design exists because a response body can be large or streamed and isn't loaded into memory just because the headers arrived. Forgetting this second await is a common source of 'why is my data a pending promise' confusion.

exercises.prompt: This function is supposed to throw a clear error when a request fails, but callers report it never seems to notice failed requests -- it just returns whatever error data the server sent, without complaint. Find and fix the bug.
hints: await fetch(...) resolving without throwing doesn't mean the request 'succeeded' in the sense you care about. What does fetch's promise reject for?
A 404 or 500 response is still a resolved promise from fetch's perspective. You need to check something on the response object to detect it.
response.ok is a boolean meant for this check. What should getProduct do when it's false?
exercises.solutionExplanation: await fetch(...) only throws for network-level failures, not for a completed request that carries an error status. A 404 response resolves normally, so the original code parses and returns the (likely error-message) body as if it were valid data, and the try/catch never notices a problem. Adding if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(...) } turns 'the server said this request failed' into a thrown error, at the point where getProduct can see the response's status. The surrounding try/catch (or an outer .catch()) then works as intended, because there's something for it to catch.

exercises.prompt: Write an async function `getJson(url)` that: performs a GET fetch to url; throws a descriptive Error (including the HTTP status code in its message) if the response is not ok; otherwise returns the parsed JSON body. Network failures (fetch itself rejecting) should propagate, with no special handling.
hints: Start with a plain await fetch(url). If the network fails, that line already throws on its own.
Right after that, check response.ok, and if it's false, throw your own Error that includes response.status in the message (a template literal is convenient).
Only after that check passes should you await response.json() and return its result.
exercises.solutionExplanation: await fetch(url) is not wrapped in a try/catch inside getJson. If it rejects because of a network failure, that rejection propagates out of getJson (since getJson is async, a throw inside it becomes a rejection of the promise it returns), so the caller's own try/catch around getJson(...) catches it, with no extra code in getJson. The if (!response.ok) check handles the case fetch doesn't treat as a failure, an HTTP error status, by throwing a new Error with the status code, which becomes the rejection reason of getJson's promise. Only when both failure modes are ruled out does the function await response.json() and return the parsed data.

assessments.prompt:
```javascript
const response = await fetch("/api/does-not-exist");
```
If the server responds with a 404 status, what happens on this line?
options: The fetch promise resolves normally with a Response object whose status is 404 and whose ok property is false.
response ends up as null.
The fetch promise rejects, and this line throws.
fetch automatically retries the request a few times before giving up.
assessments.explanation: fetch's promise only rejects for network-level failures (no connectivity, DNS issues, CORS blocks, a dropped connection). A 404 is a completed HTTP exchange from fetch's point of view, so the promise resolves normally. The Response object reflects the failure through its own properties: status is 404, and ok (true only for 200-299) is false. The promise never rejected, which is why response.ok must be checked explicitly rather than relying on a catch block to notice this kind of failure. fetch performs no automatic retries, and response is a real object, never null, once the promise resolves.

assessments.prompt: Explain how the loading/success/error pattern from manually handling fetch maps onto what a React data-fetching hook (like a custom useUser(id) hook, or a call to a library like React Query) is doing internally.
assessments.modelAnswer: Handling a fetch call well means modeling three states over the request's lifetime: it's in flight and nothing is known yet (loading), it completed and you have usable data (success), or something went wrong, either because fetch rejected from a network failure or because you detected and threw for a bad HTTP status via response.ok (error). A hand-written async function using try/await fetch/check response.ok/catch implements that three-state model as plain control flow, without keeping the 'loading' state anywhere a UI could observe it. A React data-fetching hook does the same work (fetch the URL, await the response, check its status, parse the body, handle failures) but holds each of those states in React state (commonly isLoading, data, and error, via useState, updated inside a useEffect that starts the fetch), so a component can read that state on every render and show a spinner, the data, or an error message. Libraries like React Query extend this pattern with caching, retries, and background refetching, but the three states and the fetch-and-check-response.ok logic are still underneath. Understanding the plain-JavaScript version means none of that behavior has to be taken on faith: it's the same mechanism, wired into component state.

concepts.title: ES6+ Features
concepts.description: Template literals, optional chaining, and nullish coalescing are modern syntax additions that each solve a specific, common pain point, and the ?? vs || distinction in particular fixes a bug class involving legitimate falsy values like 0.
learningObjectives: Use template literals for string interpolation and multi-line strings.
Use optional chaining (?.) to safely access possibly-missing nested properties without manual guard checks.
Explain the difference between ?? and ||, and predict when that difference produces a different result.
Situate template literals, optional chaining, nullish coalescing, arrow functions, and let/const as part of the same modern JavaScript syntax wave.

sections.heading: Template Literals
sections.body: **Template literals** use backticks (`` ` ``) instead of quotes, and support two features string concatenation never had: **interpolation** with `${expression}`, and **multi-line strings**. Before template literals, building a string from variables meant concatenation: `"Hello, " + name + "! You have " + count + " messages."`. That's readable for two variables but degrades fast as the number of values grows, since you keep breaking out of the string to add `+` operators. The template literal version, `` `Hello, ${name}! You have ${count} messages.` ``, keeps the literal text and the dynamic parts visually distinct without the `+` noise. `${ }` accepts any expression, not just a variable name: `` `Total: ${price * quantity}` `` and `` `${isAdmin ? "Admin" : "User"}` `` both work inline. Template literals also span multiple lines with no escape needed (a literal newline inside the backticks is part of the string), where a plain string would need an explicit `\n` or concatenation across lines.

sections.heading: Optional Chaining (?.)
sections.body: Accessing a deeply nested property is risky if any link in the chain might be missing: `user.address.city` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` as soon as `user.address` is `undefined` or `null`, not just when `user` itself is. The traditional defense was a chain of manual guards, `user && user.address && user.address.city`, which gets unwieldy as the chain deepens. **Optional chaining**, `?.`, does the same job directly: `user?.address?.city` evaluates left to right, and as soon as any `?.` finds its left-hand side is `null` or `undefined`, it **short-circuits**, returning `undefined` for the whole expression instead of throwing. It also works on method calls (`user.greet?.()` calls `greet` only if it exists, otherwise evaluates to `undefined`) and on bracket access (`arr?.[0]`). Each `?.` only guards the step it's attached to: `user?.address.city` (one `?.`) still throws if `user.address` is missing, because only the `user?.` step is protected. You need a `?.` at every step you want guarded.

sections.heading: Nullish Coalescing (??) and How It Differs From ||
Part of the Same ES6+ Wave
sections.body: Template literals, optional chaining, and nullish coalescing are part of a multi-year trend in JavaScript (starting with ES6/ES2015 and continuing through yearly releases, informally called 'ES6+') of adding expressive, safer syntax for patterns developers were already writing by hand, more verbosely and with more room for error. `let`/`const` (covered in the closures/scope foundations) replaced `var`'s function scoping with block scope. Arrow functions (covered in the Functions concept) gave callbacks a predictable `this`. Destructuring and spread/rest (covered in their own concept) replaced manual property-by-property extraction and array/object copying. Optional chaining and nullish coalescing continue that trend, aimed at 'safely read something that might be missing' and 'provide a default'. None of these features adds a capability JavaScript lacked; everything they do was possible longhand. They make the common, correct way to write something shorter and harder to get subtly wrong.

examples.title: Template Literals vs Concatenation
examples.explanation: messageOld and messageNew produce the same string, but messageNew reads more directly: the literal text and the two dynamic values are visually distinct without + operators breaking up the flow. receipt shows the multi-line capability: the literal newlines between backticks become real \n characters in the resulting string, with no escape sequence or concatenation needed.

examples.title: Optional Chaining and Nullish Coalescing Together
examples.explanation: order.shipping?.trackingNumber returns undefined instead of throwing, since order.shipping doesn't exist and the ?. short-circuits there. order.customer?.phone is undefined (customer exists but has no phone property), and ?? "No phone on file" supplies a fallback because undefined is what ?? triggers on. order.discount ?? 5 returns the real value 0, since ?? only falls through on null/undefined. order.discount || 5 shows the classic bug: 0 is falsy, so || treats it as if discount were missing and replaces a meaningful 0 with 5.

misconceptions.description: ?? and || are interchangeable ways to write 'use this value, or a default if it's not set' -- pick whichever you find more readable.
misconceptions.clarification: They trigger on different conditions: || falls through on any falsy value (0, "", false, NaN, null, undefined), while ?? falls through only on null or undefined specifically. Whenever a falsy value is legitimate and should NOT be replaced (a real 0 quantity, a deliberate false toggle, an intentionally empty string), || replaces it with the fallback while ?? preserves it. They only give identical results when the value can never legitimately be anything other than null/undefined/truthy, which isn't the usual case for numbers, booleans, or strings.

misconceptions.description: Optional chaining (?.) means you never have to worry about a property-access error anywhere in that expression again.
misconceptions.clarification: Each ?. only guards the link it's attached to; it doesn't protect every step in a chain. user?.address.city still throws if user.address is null/undefined, because only the user?. step is optional; you need a ?. at every step you want protected (user?.address?.city). Optional chaining also doesn't prevent every error: calling something with ?.() that exists but isn't a function still throws a TypeError. ?. only guards against the left-hand side being null/undefined.

exercises.prompt: What does each line print?
hints: ?? only cares whether the value is null or undefined. Nothing else counts, however 'empty' it looks.
|| cares about the full falsy list. 0 and "" are both falsy, even though they're legitimate, intentional values here.
settings.timeout is explicitly null, not just missing. Does ?? treat that as 'nothing here, use the fallback' or as a value to keep?
exercises.expectedAnswer: 0 (?? preserves the real 0), 5 (|| incorrectly replaces the real 0), an empty line (?? preserves the real empty string, which prints as nothing), default label (|| incorrectly replaces the real empty string), 1000 (?? replaces null, which is what ?? triggers on).
exercises.solutionExplanation: settings.retries is 0, a falsy but meaningful value: ?? only replaces null/undefined, so it returns 0; || replaces any falsy value, so it returns the fallback 5 instead of the real 0. settings.label is "", the same situation: ?? preserves the empty string, while || treats it as missing and returns "default label". settings.timeout is explicitly null, the condition ?? is designed to catch, so ?? falls through to the fallback 1000 here, unlike the previous two cases where falling through was wrong.

exercises.prompt: This function is supposed to safely display a user's city, or 'Unknown' if any part of the address chain is missing, but it still throws when address itself is missing. Find and fix the bug.
hints: Count the ?. marks in user?.address.city. How many links in this chain are protected?
user?. protects against user itself being missing, but what protects the .city access if address turns out to be missing?
You need a ?. at every step you want guarded, not just the first one in the chain.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code has one ?., after user. That protects against user being null/undefined, but .address.city after it uses plain dot notation, so if user.address is undefined (as it is for {}, which has no address property), accessing .city on it throws a TypeError, as if there were no optional chaining for that step. Adding a second ?. (user?.address?.city) protects both links: if user is missing, the first ?. short-circuits to undefined; if user exists but address is missing, the second ?. does the same. Either way the expression becomes undefined instead of throwing, and ?? "Unknown" supplies the intended fallback.

options: A TypeError, because you can't use || with the number 0
undefined, because discountPercent doesn't exist on the object
0, correctly preserving the real value
10, because || treats 0 as falsy and replaces it with the fallback, incorrectly overriding a real, intentional 0% discount
assessments.explanation: 0 is falsy, so order.discountPercent || 10 treats an explicit 0 the same as if discountPercent were missing: it falls through to the fallback 10 and reports a 10% discount when the intended value was 0%. This is the bug class nullish coalescing (??) exists to fix: order.discountPercent ?? 10 would return 0, since ?? only falls through on null or undefined and treats a real 0 as a value worth keeping.

assessments.prompt: Explain why template literals, optional chaining, and nullish coalescing are often grouped together as 'modern JavaScript features,' and what they have in common with arrow functions and let/const, despite all doing very different things syntactically.
assessments.modelAnswer: Each of these features solves a narrow pain point that developers worked around by hand, with more verbose and more error-prone patterns, before the feature existed. Template literals replace + chains with ${} interpolation and native multi-line support. Optional chaining replaces a hand-written chain of && guards (user && user.address && user.address.city) with one ?. per step. Nullish coalescing replaces a common but subtly wrong use of || as a default-value operator with one that only triggers on null/undefined, fixing a bug class involving legitimate falsy values like 0 or an empty string. None adds a capability JavaScript lacked; everything they do was possible with older syntax. They make the common, correct version of the pattern shorter and harder to get subtly wrong. The same goes for let/const (replacing var's function scoping and hoisting behavior with block scope) and arrow functions (replacing .bind(this) or var self = this workarounds with lexical this): all are part of a multi-year trend of the language absorbing error-prone hand-written patterns into safer built-in syntax, not isolated tricks.

concepts.title: npm and JSON
concepts.description: package.json is a project's manifest of dependencies and scripts, npm install and npm run are how you act on it, semantic versioning ranges control what gets installed, and JSON itself is the same plain-text data format you've already used from Python, with different language bindings.
learningObjectives: Explain the role of package.json as a project manifest, including dependencies, devDependencies, and scripts.
Explain what npm install does and why package-lock.json is committed to version control.
Run project scripts with npm run and explain the purpose of the scripts field.
Interpret ^ and ~ semantic versioning ranges and predict which versions each would allow.
Explain that JSON is a strict, language-independent data format, and connect it to JSON already seen in Python.

sections.heading: package.json: The Project Manifest
sections.body: **`package.json`** is the file at the root of a JavaScript/Node project that describes it: its name and version, metadata like a description and license, and, most important day to day, its **dependencies**. `"dependencies"` lists packages the project needs to actually run in production (a UI library, a data-fetching helper); `"devDependencies"` lists packages only needed while developing (a test runner, a linter, a build tool) that don't need to ship with the finished application. Every one of these is recorded as a package name mapped to a version range (covered below). This file is the project's source of truth for 'what does this project depend on, and how do you build/run/test it', so anyone who clones the project can read package.json and know both.

sections.heading: npm install and Running Scripts
sections.body:
**`npm install`** (often just `npm i`) reads `package.json`'s dependencies and `devDependencies`, resolves a compatible version for each one (and for every dependency those dependencies need, recursively), downloads them into a `node_modules` folder, and writes (or updates) a **`package-lock.json`** file recording the *exact* version of every package that was installed, down to the deepest nested dependency. That lockfile is what makes builds reproducible: without it, two developers (or a developer's machine and a CI server) running `npm install` against the same `package.json` at different times could resolve different versions if anything in the dependency tree published an update in between. `package-lock.json` pins the tree that was resolved, so everyone gets the same versions. That is why `package-lock.json` is committed to version control, while `node_modules` almost never is (it can be regenerated from the lockfile, and it's typically enormous).

The `"scripts"` field in `package.json` maps short names to actual shell commands: `"scripts": { "dev": "vite", "test": "jest", "build": "vite build" }`. Running `npm run dev` executes whatever command is mapped to `"dev"`. (A few names get a shortcut: `npm start` and `npm test` work without the word `run`, as do `npm stop` and `npm restart`; everything else needs the full `npm run <name>`.) This way a team doesn't need to agree on raw tool invocations. Everyone runs `npm run build` whatever tool or flags it maps to underneath, and the mapping can change without anyone changing their habits.

sections.heading: Semantic Versioning: ^ and ~
sections.body: Package versions generally follow **semantic versioning** (semver): `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, e.g. `4.17.21` -- `MAJOR` increments for breaking changes, `MINOR` for backward-compatible features, `PATCH` for backward-compatible bug fixes. The prefix in front of a version in `package.json` controls how much automatic upgrade `npm install` may pick: **`^4.17.21`** (caret, the default npm writes) allows any version that doesn't change the leftmost non-zero number -- so it can install up to (but not including) `5.0.0`: any `MINOR` or `PATCH` update is fine, but no `MAJOR` bump. **`~4.17.21`** (tilde) is more conservative: it only allows `PATCH`-level updates, up to (but not including) `4.18.0`. An exact version with no prefix (`4.17.21`) allows no automatic updates. For example, with `"lodash": "^4.17.21"` in `package.json`, if `4.17.25` and `5.0.0` both exist, a fresh `npm install` picks `4.17.25` (a patch update, allowed) and never `5.0.0` (a major bump, not allowed by `^`). With `~4.17.21` instead, only patch-level releases like `4.17.25` are allowed; a hypothetical `4.18.0` (a minor bump) would not be, even though `^` would allow it.

sections.heading: JSON as a Data Interchange Format
sections.body:
`package.json` is itself written in **JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation), but JSON is not JavaScript-specific, despite the name and despite looking almost like a JavaScript object literal. It's a plain-text data format with its own strict rules, used for things unrelated to JavaScript: API responses, configuration files, data exports, and `package.json` itself. JSON supports objects (`{ }`), arrays (`[ ]`), strings (always double-quoted), numbers, `true`/`false`, and `null`, and nothing else. It is **stricter** than a JavaScript object literal: every key must be a double-quoted string (unquoted or single-quoted keys are invalid JSON, though valid in a JS object literal), and there are no comments, no trailing commas, and no way to represent a function, `undefined`, or a `Symbol`.

If you've studied Python in this same app, you've already used this format there: `json.loads()`/`json.dumps()` read and write the same JSON text with the same rules, and JavaScript's equivalents are `JSON.parse()` (text to a JS value) and `JSON.stringify()` (a JS value to text). Same format, same rules, different languages on either side. That is the point of JSON as a format: a neutral, language-independent way for systems written in different languages to exchange structured data without caring what language produced or will consume it.

examples.title: A Minimal package.json
examples.explanation: react and react-dom sit under dependencies because the built application needs them at runtime in the browser. vite (the build tool) and jest (the test runner) sit under devDependencies because they're only needed while developing and building; the shipped app doesn't need them to run. npm run dev executes vite (the command mapped to the "dev" script name); npm test works without the word run, since test is one of the few script names npm recognizes directly.

examples.title: ^ vs ~ With Concrete Available Versions
examples.explanation: ^1.4.0 allows any update that keeps the leftmost non-zero version number (1, the MAJOR version) unchanged, so both the PATCH bump to 1.4.5 and the MINOR bump to 1.6.0 are allowed, and npm picks the highest, 1.6.0; the MAJOR bump to 2.0.0 is excluded because ^ never crosses that boundary. ~1.4.0 is more restrictive: it only allows PATCH-level updates within the same MINOR version (1.4.x), so 1.4.5 is allowed but 1.6.0 (a MINOR bump) is not, and npm picks 1.4.5 as the highest version in that narrower range.

misconceptions.description: JSON and a JavaScript object literal are exactly the same thing, so it's fine to add comments or use single-quoted/unquoted keys in a .json file.
misconceptions.clarification: JSON is a stricter subset of what a JavaScript object literal can express, even though the two look very similar. Valid JSON requires every key and string value to be wrapped in double quotes (not single quotes, and keys can't be left unquoted), allows no comments, and allows no trailing comma after the last item in an object or array. A JavaScript object literal permits all of those (unquoted keys, single quotes, trailing commas, JS comments), but a .json file, or anything passed to JSON.parse, does not; a JSON parser throws a syntax error on any of them.
misconceptions.fact: JSON is a stricter subset of what a JavaScript object literal can express, even though the two look very similar.

misconceptions.description: ^1.2.3 and ~1.2.3 mean roughly the same thing -- both just mean 'approximately this version, updates are fine.'
misconceptions.clarification: They allow different ranges of automatic updates. ^1.2.3 allows any MINOR or PATCH update, up to (but not including) the next MAJOR version, so it would accept 1.9.0. ~1.2.3 only allows PATCH-level updates within the same MINOR version: it would accept 1.2.9 but not 1.3.0. Given the same published versions, ^ and ~ can resolve to different installed versions, which matters when a MINOR release introduces a bug or behavior change you'd rather not pick up automatically.

exercises.prompt: A package.json has `"chart-lib": "~2.3.0"`. The published versions available on the registry are 2.3.0, 2.3.4, 2.4.0, and 3.0.0. Which version does a fresh `npm install` pick, and why?
hints: ~ only allows updates within the same MINOR version number, which here means staying within the 2.3.x line.
2.4.0 changes the MINOR number (2.3 to 2.4). Does ~ allow crossing that boundary?
Among the allowed versions, npm picks the highest one available, not just any matching one.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 2.3.4, the highest version that stays within the same MINOR line (2.3.x); 2.4.0 and 3.0.0 are both excluded because ~ only allows PATCH-level updates.
exercises.solutionExplanation: ~2.3.0 permits only PATCH-level updates with MAJOR.MINOR fixed at 2.3, so any 2.3.x is allowed, but 2.4.0 (a MINOR bump) and 3.0.0 (a MAJOR bump) are outside the range. 2.3.0 and 2.3.4 both satisfy 2.3.x, and npm resolves to the highest satisfying version, so it picks 2.3.4.

exercises.prompt: This file is meant to be a valid config.json, but a JSON.parse() call on its contents throws a SyntaxError. Find every problem preventing it from being valid JSON and rewrite it correctly.
hints: JSON requires every key to be wrapped in double quotes. Is name written that way here?
Single-quoted strings aren't valid JSON, though they're valid JavaScript. What does 'weather-app' need to become?
Look for two more problems: something JSON has no syntax for (a line explaining what timeout means), and something left after the last property that JSON doesn't allow.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Four problems, all common when someone writes JSON as if it were a JS object literal: name was an unquoted key (JSON requires double-quoted keys); 'weather-app' used single quotes (JSON strings must be double-quoted); the // comment line has no equivalent in JSON, which has no comment syntax, and a parser fails on it rather than skipping it; and the trailing comma after "retries": 3 is invalid, since JSON does not allow a comma after the last property in an object (or the last element in an array). The corrected version double-quotes name and its value, removes the comment, and deletes the trailing comma.

assessments.prompt: A package.json lists `"some-lib": "^2.5.0"`. Which of the following newly published versions would npm install be allowed to pick?
assessments.explanation: ^2.5.0 allows any MINOR or PATCH update that keeps the leftmost non-zero number (the MAJOR version, 2) unchanged, so anything from 2.5.0 up to (but not including) 3.0.0 is allowed. 2.9.1 fits that range. 3.0.0 is excluded because it's a MAJOR bump, which ^ refuses to cross. 1.9.9 is an older MAJOR version, not a valid upgrade target. 2.4.9 is older than the specified 2.5.0 minimum, so it wouldn't be selected either; the range only covers versions from 2.5.0 upward.

assessments.prompt: Someone who has only used Python's json module asks whether JavaScript's JSON.parse/JSON.stringify are 'basically the same idea.' Explain how JSON as a format relates to the two languages.
assessments.modelAnswer: JSON is not tied to either language. It's a plain-text data format with its own strict grammar (objects, arrays, double-quoted strings, numbers, true/false, null, and nothing beyond that), designed so that programs written in different languages can exchange structured data without knowing what language the other side uses. Python's json.loads() and JavaScript's JSON.parse() do the same job: turn that text into the language's native in-memory structures (a Python dict/list, or a JS object/array), and json.dumps() and JSON.stringify() do the reverse. So yes, it's 'basically the same idea' in the strongest sense: not a similar idea implemented twice, but the same wire format and rules, with each language providing its own pair of functions to read and write it. One caveat: a JSON file is stricter than either language's native literal syntax (no comments, no trailing commas, keys must be double-quoted strings), so both parsers reject JSON text that uses Python-style single-quoted strings or JavaScript-style unquoted keys, even though both would be valid in that language's own dict or object literal syntax.
